004ba9b7-31c0-504f-8fe8-703d886502ce.description2: This 500 piastres bank note bears no watermark, and is illustrated with horses, symbolising pride, and Cedar trees, the national tree.

00dfb034-7745-571e-9003-aff48bf346d0.name: Talismanic necklace
00dfb034-7745-571e-9003-aff48bf346d0.type: Amulet; cultic object; talismanic object; jewellery

00dfb034-7745-571e-9003-aff48bf346d0.description2: A triangular silver pendant decorated with small circles on the top and five blue beads with five silver Ottoman coins dangling at the end, and a silver chain known traditionally as “heal of gazelle”. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom.

01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.name: Portrait of Abraham Salamon De Camondo
01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.holder: The Quincentennial Foundation Museum, Zulfaris Synagogue Museum
01a64f5c-ceca-5e43-b3af-115b31492d64.description2: The Camondo Family is a family of Spanish-Portuguese Jewish origin. Abraham Salomon Camondo, who was born in İstanbul in 1781, acted as the Ottoman government's banker before the establishment of the Ottoman Bank. He founded a bank called "*Isaac et Compagnie Camondo*" with his brother Isaac in 1815. The bank grew in a short time period into a reputable international financial institution. Camondo prospered greatly and became the prime banker to the Ottoman Empire until the founding of the Imperial Ottoman Bank in 1863. The bank had a close relationship with the business community and banks of London, Paris and the Vienna Stock Exchange. The bank had also funded defence needs of Ottoman Empire during the Crimean War.

01e7089c-8585-5199-92a7-c9b05620637b.name: [Paris] stock exchange
01e7089c-8585-5199-92a7-c9b05620637b.description2: This building (Palais Brongniart), located in the heart of Paris, housed the French stock exchange for almost two centuries. Its atmosphere, as a powerful financial building bearing witness to great bankers' fortunes and failures, inspired writers such as Honoré de Balzac in La Maison Nucingen and Émile Zola in L’Argent.

02125310-0cbe-5f6f-833f-c178410397b3.name: Official document regarding the connection of Beirut–Damascus railway line to Beirut Port
02125310-0cbe-5f6f-833f-c178410397b3.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
02125310-0cbe-5f6f-833f-c178410397b3.description2: This document concerns the connection of the Beirut- Damascus railway line to Beirut port. It was signed during a large ceremony inaugurating the connection of railway lines across the country.

025b84b0-d00d-5c21-a749-98f3596f9d77.name: Boots
025b84b0-d00d-5c21-a749-98f3596f9d77.description: Men’s leather riding boots. The applications of leather in different colours, with representation of geometric patterns, follow the customs and superstitions of the Hausa. The Hausa possessed, in every community, workshops for producing and dyeing articles of leather, though the most out-standing locations are those of Kano and Sokoto in Nigeria; places producing, since the medieval times, the thinnest skins used in Europe. The skins are those of goat, preferably of the males, and the dye receives the local name of *bagaruwa*. This product is usually processed by women, and it is also used for treating dysentery. The products of the Hausa are distributed, by trade, across wide zones of the Sahel and Subsaharian Africa.

02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.name: The Coffee Shop of Cairo
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.description2: This colourful print depicts a typical 19th century coffeeshop in Cairo. An exclusively male domain, its design was characterised by an open front and wide benches for seating, to allow for easy congregation and the gathering of friends and acquainances. Not only in Cairo, which had over a thousands coffeehouses in Roberts's time, but all over the Middle East, coffeehouses were important social hubs for the exchange of news, entertainment, smoking (customers brought their own pipes and waterpipes) and - not rarely - political dissent. Musicians and storytellers often enhanced the experience further. In this image, the proprietor or an employee of the cafe can be seen serving a beverage in the centre. Interestingly, both the ewer and the large copper cup he uses are of a type usually associated with water, not coffee. Perhaps Roberts introduced these items for artistic effect.
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.artist_birthplace: David Roberts: Edinburgh, Scotland; Louis Hague: Tournai, Belgium
02c23c32-bafe-5d35-af62-5391f4a033ad.artist_deathplace: David Roberts: London; Louis Hague: London

03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.name: Necklace
03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.keywords: zebra fish; concave; Ottoman; coins; silver
03fa93d0-4ba6-5345-9362-3c66f5efb5d1.description2: A zebra fish chain with a concave silver Turkish coins and two metal circles at the end to fix the necklace on the hat and dangle down the neck. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. Jordan's economy relied on trade and crafts; new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for these purposes. This object reflects the diverse population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also demonstrates personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.name: The Silk Factory
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.history: The silk industry was a very important part of the Lebanese economy - the transportation of silk and silk cocoons from Beirut to Marseille, for example, laid the foundations for maritime trade agencies in Lebanon. The loans and grants made to intermediaries and traders wishing to buy silk cocoons from farmers were some of the first financial traders, which later led to the establishment of the first Lebanese bank and to the development of the Port of Beirut. In Gaston Ducousso's book, *The Silk Industry in Syria and Lebanon*, published in 1912, the French Consul in Beirut counted no less than 183 spinning mills in Lebanon. In 1841, a team of spinners was brought from France to train young women in the art of spinning silk, something which was particularly foreign to the rural areas, where young women were not traditionally employed in this form of labour.
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.architects: Prosper, Nicolas, Joseph and Antoine Fortuné Portalis
05d601e6-b672-5f09-a5af-f912a7e4475e.description2: In 1841, Prosper, Nicolas, Joseph and Antoine Fortuné Portalis built the first spinning mill for reeling cocoons, in Btater in the Chouf region.

0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.name: Captain's Pearl Chest containing his most precious possessions, including folding pearl gauges with 44 grades, knife for opening oysters, weight set and hand compass
0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.dimensions: Length 532 mm, depth 301 mm, height 193 mm
0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.materials: Teak wood, iron, copper alloy, textile
0703f771-513c-549f-8e72-02d81616e8d9.description2: This pearl merchant's chest, known in the region as bishtakha, was an indispensable item of a pearl merchant's profession, as it contained not only all his equipment, but also his valuable bags of pearls. Made of hardwood and often elaborately decorated, these chests could come in different sizes and were designed to hold pearling scales with their agate weights, scoops, graded sieves, small discrete boxes for cash - often hidden in secret compartments - bags of pearls and the so-called chao book, used to calculate - by means of detailed tables - the value of specific pearls on the basis of their weight.

078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.name: *Bayt Niyadu, Damascus*
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.second_name: Inhabitants in the courtyard demonstrating the new style of decoration and clothing
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.description2: Like the Lisbuna House, Bayt Niyadu saw two major construction phases, namely, in the 18th and late 19th century. It was refurbished as so many houses between 1865 and 1872 and features marble ornamentation similar to the one in Bayt Lisbuna´s courtyard. These houses are from the layout typical "traditional" courtyard houses of the region. However, the Niyadu House became known (also on postcards) for its richness and abundance of up to date Ottoman decor. The owners expressed their Damascene modernity proudly to the outside – also in this picture: the gentlemen sports a European-style dinner jacket and the lady a mid-length skirt, teamed with a withe blouse in the latest fashion. This transformation of private forms of urban live – notice also the brand new and modern electrical lightening in the "traditional" courtyard – can be seen throughout the city and is an important example of a local expression of global modernity.

0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.name: Misrata [Libya]. In the Home of Gabrielli, Agent of the Society of Maritime Services [Società dei servizi marittimi]
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.third_name: *Misràta. In casa di Gabrielli, agente della Società dei servizi marittimi*
0b6eceea-2f90-5eb6-9483-03f0734b34dc.description2:
In 19th and early 20th century Africa, the nature of the relations between European men and African women varied dramatically according to the different power relations between the partners. In colonial situations, the legal subordination of the colonised people put African women in particularly weak positions vis-à-vis European men, generally resulting in very exploitative relationships. In countries that were not under European rule, more balanced relationships could develop.  
This picture shows a mixed family in Libya before the onset of Italian colonialism. The setting of the picture suggests that the Libyan woman enjoyed respect and status within the family: the woman and her children are sitting on chairs, surrounded by persons who appear to be domestic servants, and the Italian man is standing behind her, looking at their children.

0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.name: Earrings
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.author: Huda Kilani
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.keywords: 23 karat gold; rosettes; coral; Ottoman coins
0ba2e663-9318-562e-9c2a-099d167e8112.description2: 23-karat gold earrings from South Palestine (Beer Sheba), with red stones, blue talismans mounted on rosettes of coral, and gold Ottoman coins (dated 1808). Silver jewellery was the most common because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. Silver or gold jewellery was part of the dowry given by the groom to the bride. The material (gold or silver) and even the coins used as pieces of jewellery were an indirect statement of the financial status of the groom.

0c6f934e-a89f-5201-8884-4f5cd43e4cba.name: Turkish weights
0c6f934e-a89f-5201-8884-4f5cd43e4cba.description2: After Wallachia and Moldavia entered under Ottoman sovereignty and the Ottoman Empire became their main commercial partner, a series of Ottoman measures of mass and weight were adopted, such as the “oka” (1.282 kg) or the “kantar” (56.449 kg). When in 1864 the Romanian Ministry of Agriculture decreed the introduction in the United Principalities of the metric system, all the measures used in the past were abolished.

0e7a0149-6b93-507e-b4df-dc55cdc5bd9f.name: Iron coffee roasting spoon
0e7a0149-6b93-507e-b4df-dc55cdc5bd9f.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
0e7a0149-6b93-507e-b4df-dc55cdc5bd9f.author: Huda Kilani
0e7a0149-6b93-507e-b4df-dc55cdc5bd9f.keywords: coffee; coffee roasting; coffee beans; domestic furnishing; domestic vessels
0e7a0149-6b93-507e-b4df-dc55cdc5bd9f.description2: Iron coffee roasting spoon used to turn coffee beans while roasting them. Coffee-drinking in a communal setting is an essential part of traditions in Bedouin communities to celebrate or mourn.

0e9e0841-ee1f-5aa8-8944-2225bf18b5d7.name: Coffee pot
0e9e0841-ee1f-5aa8-8944-2225bf18b5d7.holder: Sharjah Heritage Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
0e9e0841-ee1f-5aa8-8944-2225bf18b5d7.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
0e9e0841-ee1f-5aa8-8944-2225bf18b5d7.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
0e9e0841-ee1f-5aa8-8944-2225bf18b5d7.description2: This copper dallah goes back to a type allegedly first used in 17th-century Baghdad, By the 19th century, we know of several production centres in the Arabian peninsula. Its design reflects its functional needs. The broad base ensures stability on the fire or on the sand, the large beak prevents too much coffee sediment to reach the cup. The lid is weighted to avoid it opening during the pouring process.The quality and quantity of the coffee served indicated the wealth of the host and status of the guest. Throughout the Near and Middle East coffee lay at the heart of social ritual and hospitality, while providing sustenance during chats, debate and political discourse in the many coffeehouses in the region. In continental Europe, the fashion for coffee was at its height in the 17th and 18th centuries, with coffeehouses the preferred meeting places for intellectuals and artists. In Britain, meanwhile, tea soon overtook coffee in popularity, even though certain religious organisations tried to promote coffee houses for the poor in order to steer them away from pubs and bars.

0ee9442b-fe87-5668-a98a-944398b82de9.name: *Egypt. Suez canal.*
0ee9442b-fe87-5668-a98a-944398b82de9.keywords: Suez canal; Egypt; Ferdinand de Lesseps
0ee9442b-fe87-5668-a98a-944398b82de9.second_name: Taken from the collection *Lithiographies Représentant L'isthme de Suez*
0ee9442b-fe87-5668-a98a-944398b82de9.description2: The inauguration of the Suez Canal saw spectacular celebrations, attended by many European royalties. This was a huge victory for Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had sincerely hoped it would be a memorable and historical event. On his request, the painter Édouard Riou (1833–1900) produced a series of watercolours which were later published in *L’Album de l’Impératrice : Voyage Pittoresque à travers l’Isthme de Suez*.

0fa95d00-46ca-5bec-8348-9b86a0617d78.name: Ten Ottoman piasters
0fa95d00-46ca-5bec-8348-9b86a0617d78.author: Aida Naghawi
0fa95d00-46ca-5bec-8348-9b86a0617d78.description2: On obverse *tuğra* of sultan Abdul Hamid II, flower to right, denomination below: ١٠ ش “10 sh”, all within wreath with crossed quivers and unstrung bow at bottom, above seven stars, “W” below wreath tie. On reverse: within a wreath: “*duriba fi misr* 1293 22” (“22, struck in Misr, 1293”). Above 3 stars. It was issued in the year 22 (AH 1317 / AD 1896) of sultan Abdul Hamid II’s reign (Hegira 1293–1327 / AD 1876–1909).

109c897b-cb5d-5bc6-9360-7b2423876f34.name: Romanian coin – 10 bani 1867
109c897b-cb5d-5bc6-9360-7b2423876f34.description2: In October 1866, when the sultan recognized the reign of Carol I of Hohenzollern, the Principalities were given the right to struck national coins, but on one condition, namely that a sign symbolizing the Ottoman Empire, the Principalities’ suzerain, had to appear on the coins. Despite this, when the Romanian Parliament adopted the Law for the establishment of a Romanian monetary system and for the making of national coins (April 1867), it was decided that the coins would bear no inscription referring to the sovereign power. The first coins issued based on this monetary law were commissioned that same year to two British Mints, Heaton Mint and Watt & Comp. They were made of copper and their design belonged to British engraver Leonard Charles Wyon.

109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.name: Drum
109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.author: Huda Kilani
109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.keywords: drum; animals skin; linen rope; wooden stick; Ramadan; to wake up
109ed34a-507a-5652-bb30-736569eca0ac.description2: Small round drum, pointed on the bottom, covered on the top with leather, and fastened with a linen rope. It was played with a wooden stick to create special sounds of music, and it was used during the Muslim holy month of Ramadan to wake up people to eat (*suhur*) before sunrise. Some people used to volunteer to go around before dawn to wake people up during Holy Ramadan, reflecting community spirit.

11048de0-74f3-54a9-a02b-fa1ad1add1c1.name: Moroccan coins
11048de0-74f3-54a9-a02b-fa1ad1add1c1.description: Coin struck in 1936 under Sultan Mulay Yusuf (reigned twice, first in 1927-53 and then again in 1955-61) at the Paris mint. For a century (1800-1900) the ‘Alawid sultans struck coins in the workshops of Fez, but due to the economic crisis at the time, gold was unavailable so most coins were of silver, bronze or other common metals – although the technique remained the same, with the metal poured into moulds. The patterns on the face and on the back vary between the star with eight points (Solomon ring) and the indication of the place of mint.

11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.name: Winter jacket
11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.author: Huda Kilani
11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.materials: Wool, cotton and silk; hand weaving and hand embroidered
11568132-d5af-54cf-9a3f-f663abfb4f5b.description2: Sleeveless jacket made of woollen fabric of red and black stripes, decorated with floral motifs of orange and purple colour with couching in silk threads on the shoulders and the bottom. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, influenced by the local economy. The main activities were trade and crafts that influenced population movements and the coexistence of various local and foreign communities.

1223f05d-519a-50c0-8c79-8e8c02636ede.name: Chandelier
1223f05d-519a-50c0-8c79-8e8c02636ede.holder: Shangri La, Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art
1223f05d-519a-50c0-8c79-8e8c02636ede.keywords: glass; chandelier; France; Baccarat; India; Salar Jung; collector; collection
1223f05d-519a-50c0-8c79-8e8c02636ede.description2: During the nineteenth century, a vogue developed in western and southern Asia for European glass. Manufacturers such as Baccarat in France responded to these markets by producing glassware with motifs and aesthetics that they believed would appeal to these new consumers. This chandelier is thought to have been made for export to India. Indeed, Doris Duke purchased the chandelier in 1966 from the estate of Salar Jung, a noted collector in Hyderabad, India.

124efc2d-1a23-56df-83e7-543dbb950692.name: Port of Beirut
124efc2d-1a23-56df-83e7-543dbb950692.description: The Port of Beirut is the main port in Lebanon and it is one of the most beneficial commercial architecture in Lebanon that contributes the state’s revenue. It was founded in 1887 under the reign of the Ottomans and has since been the western-eastern link in the Middle East area. The Port of Beirut has a total area of 1,200,000 m2.
124efc2d-1a23-56df-83e7-543dbb950692.holder: Government of Lebanon; Gestation and exploitation of Port of Beirut (GEPB)
124efc2d-1a23-56df-83e7-543dbb950692.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Rita El Hachem, Julien El Khoury
124efc2d-1a23-56df-83e7-543dbb950692.history: Founded in 1887, the Port of Beirut is located on the eastern side of St Georges Bay, on Beirut's northern Mediterranean coast, west of the Beirut river. It is one of the largest and busiest ports of the Eastern Mediterranean. In early 90’s, a phase of development and reconstruction took place. The Port was rehabilitated and expanded to encompass 4 docks, 2 new quays (15 and 16) and new container terminal with 700,000 TEU/year capacities. The container terminal became operational in February 2005. It is equipped with 6 ship-to-shore gantry cranes (outreach 60m) and 18 rubbed tyred gantry cranes. The Port of Beirut has been selected as a transhipment hub for the 2nd and 3rd largest container shipping companies in the world.

138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.name: *View of Constantinople*
138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.author: Papastratos 1990, vol. 2, 578-79, figs. 617-18; Delivorrias, Fotopoulos 1997, 508-9, figs. 900-901
138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.description2: Both this print and the *View of Smyrna* are based on earlier Western ones, which have been assimilated into the distinctive Athonite topographical style. They are exceptions to the corpus of Athonite prints, since they are of secular subjects. The printmaker was, indeed, active outside Athos, where he executed nonreligious commissions. The subjects relate to the tradition of topographical murals depicting important commercial and cultural centers of the day that decorated the mansions of wealthy merchants by the mid-eighteenth century. Kaldis aimed to supply a wider public with inexpensive works of a decorative nature. The activity of merchants from Lesbos at Smyrna, Constantinople, and the Black Sea on the one hand justified the choice of subject and, on the other, provided the appropriate network in which the multiple printed works could circulate. In order to attract the largest possible clientele, the view is coloured and annotated with explanatory comments in Greek and Turkish.

en: Delivorrias, Angelos, and Fotopoulos, Dionisis, *Greece at the Benaki Museum*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1997.
Papastratos, Dory, *Paper Icons: Greek Orthodox Religious Engravings, 1665–1899*, vol. 2, Athens: Papastratos, 1990.

16e62e70-a7b1-5c81-b4f3-e37bfa439cad.name: Letter by Kenny Leveck to Odeh Goussous
16e62e70-a7b1-5c81-b4f3-e37bfa439cad.description: A unique document signed by Kenny Leveck. The document is dispatched to the attorney general Mr. Odeh-Goussous informing him that the president of the high council of Kerak's national government appointed him attorney general on 21 September, 1920, asking him to take up his position seriously and actively. At the end of the letter is the signature “chief of high council, British resident, Major Kenny Leveck,” then a stamp of Kenny Leveck in Arabic. To the right is the translation of the signature in English, "F.M Kenny leveck, A political officer and president of council, Kerak." (The letter A means Acting.) Kenny Leveck was in Kerak for a couple of weeks, where he headed the new administration formed from the Elders of the Kerak Tribes known as “the National Government of Moab”. It is not true what Sir Alec Seath Kirkbirde mentioned in his book *A Crackle of Thorns*, page 21-22, that he was elected by the council of Kerak and became head of the High Council of Kerak, or as he says on page 22, he “became head of a more less independent republic”.
16e62e70-a7b1-5c81-b4f3-e37bfa439cad.author: Aida Naghawi
16e62e70-a7b1-5c81-b4f3-e37bfa439cad.keywords: Attorney general; Odeh-Goussous; High council; Kerak national government

179af9eb-b888-57e9-b30c-78f45dee8021.name: *Weapons Market Street*
179af9eb-b888-57e9-b30c-78f45dee8021.keywords: Weapons Market; Cairo Markets; Old Cairo
179af9eb-b888-57e9-b30c-78f45dee8021.description2: A rare photo of the weapons market street that goes back more than 700 years and is located in the Darb al-Ahmar area, to the North of Cairo. It was originally called “Al-`Izzi Market”, after a relative to Prince `Izz al-Din Bahdar, one of the Bahri Mamluks who was said to live there. With the passing of time, people started calling it “Suq al-Silah" street because of its many workshops and factories that made a variety of different weapons, including spears, swords and shields. The street provided weapons to the Citadel during the Mamluk era in Egypt.

17b041f8-8464-54a0-bfab-c18e51639102.name: A rare photo showing important guests at the inauguration of Luxor–Aswan Railway Line
17b041f8-8464-54a0-bfab-c18e51639102.description2: A group of guests at the inauguration of the Luxor–Aswan Railway Line upon disembarking at the Station of Aswan. One of the rare photos for the inauguration of the Luxor–Aswan railway line, with `Adli Yakan Pasha; Muhammad Najib al-Gharabli Pasha; Husayn Rushdi Pasha; Tharwat Pasha; Fathallah Barakat Pasha; Morkos Hanna Pasha; al-Dagwi Bek, director of Aswan; and Mahmud Shakir Bek, deputy undersecretary of the Ministry of Transportation in attendance, in 1926.

18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.name: Dagger
18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.dimensions: Length without sheath 28 cm, sheath length 19.5 cm
18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.author: Huda Kilani
18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.keywords: Thin silver; Hammering; sheath; geometric motifs; turquoise; arms; armours; metalwork; fashion; accessories
18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.materials: Thin silver, wood, metal; casting handmade
18e02623-b9ad-5163-8ba9-d958a15a6f01.description2: Wooden handled dagger with thin silver sheath; incurved geometric designs on the obverse side; inset with turquoise and black stones. The dagger was used by both Bedouins and villagers as part of men’s traditional garb. This object reflects the diverse population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also demonstrates personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

19dba65f-a9fe-593e-8561-b4a20b42b083.name: *A British Ship Coral Fishing Near Algiers*
19dba65f-a9fe-593e-8561-b4a20b42b083.author: Rossana Spadaccini, Cristina Francioli
19dba65f-a9fe-593e-8561-b4a20b42b083.archival: ASNa, Ministero degli affari esteri, Piante, 7048
19dba65f-a9fe-593e-8561-b4a20b42b083.third_name: *Bastimento inglese esercitando la pesca del corallo*
19dba65f-a9fe-593e-8561-b4a20b42b083.description2: Coral fishing was an important economic activity in the Mediterranean. Algeria was the main fishing area for corals, especially after the depletion of Sardinian coral, and ships from different countries competed for this valuable resource. Torre del Greco, near Naples, was the most important port town for coral fishing in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, while Livorno was the most important port town for coral fishing in the Grand Duke of Tuscany. In 1864, Torre del Greco had 300 coral-fishing boats while Livorno had 60.

1a477c20-c077-5125-9fc1-9d8eb04e2681.name: *View in the Plain of Latakia, in Syria*
1a477c20-c077-5125-9fc1-9d8eb04e2681.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
1a477c20-c077-5125-9fc1-9d8eb04e2681.provenance: First published in Robert Brown, *The Countries of the World*, published by Cassell and Company Ltd, London and New York, 1876, p. 28
1a477c20-c077-5125-9fc1-9d8eb04e2681.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
1a477c20-c077-5125-9fc1-9d8eb04e2681.description2: This print, entitled 'View in the Plain of Latakia, Syria' was first published on page 28 of in Robert Brown''s 'The Countries of the World', published by Cassell and Company Ltd, London and New York in 1876. In the 19th century, Latakia was famous for its tobacco, grown in the plain behind the town and on the Ansarieh hills. Three main varieties of tobacco were produced: the lowest quality was dark in colour and strong in flavour; the best, grown in the districts of Diryus and Amamareh, was light and aromatic, exported mainly to Alexandria, Constantinople, Cyprus and directly to Europe.

1ca3c828-bf7a-599e-a4f4-bc69d80d6a00.name: A photograph of the old building of the Berlin Stock Exchange
1ca3c828-bf7a-599e-a4f4-bc69d80d6a00.holder: Photo archives of the Prussian Heritage Foundation

1d05a82c-6016-572a-b4ab-6100639104d3.name: Project for a steamship for the Sultan of Morocco, by the Fratelli Orlando shipyards (Livorno, Italy)
1d05a82c-6016-572a-b4ab-6100639104d3.author: Daniela Tazzi
1d05a82c-6016-572a-b4ab-6100639104d3.archival: ASLi, Cantiere Navale Luigi Orlando, busta 10M2
1d05a82c-6016-572a-b4ab-6100639104d3.description2:
Project drawn to a scale 1:100.  
In 1899, the Fratelli Orlando shipyards (Livorno, Italy) made a project of a screw steamer for the Sultan of Morocco. The steamer was to have two decks, two steam engines of 900 HP and harbour twelve passengers. The project, however, was never realised.  
The Fratelli Orlando shipyards built the cruiser Bascir for the Moroccan Navy and a yacht for the Khédivé of Egypt.

1d3af9a9-da3f-50ca-95c3-42bd8920651e.name: Medwakh Pipe
1d3af9a9-da3f-50ca-95c3-42bd8920651e.holder: Sharjah Heritage Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
1d3af9a9-da3f-50ca-95c3-42bd8920651e.dates: Hegira first half of the 14th century / AD first half of the 20th century
1d3af9a9-da3f-50ca-95c3-42bd8920651e.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
1d3af9a9-da3f-50ca-95c3-42bd8920651e.description2: This small pipe has a long tradition among the local sailors and seafarers in the Gulf region, who traditionally favoured Medwakh tobacco, a particular local blend mixed with herbs, spices and aromatic bark. It was produced locally and came in three strengths, from cold (barid) to warm (dafi) and hot (har). Unlike other tobaccos, dokha, as it is known as, is not harvested and cured, its vegetal ingredients simply dried in the sun. As the dokha mixtures were very potent, they were only ever smoked in very small pipes like the one illustrated here.

1df2efa8-09f6-56fe-b40d-5cff853bf496.name: Revolver
1df2efa8-09f6-56fe-b40d-5cff853bf496.description: A Belgian produced double action revolver, serial number 6647, with a five-shot cylinder. Fitted with chequered wooden grips, this revolver features some simple leaf and scroll pattern and border engraving of the frame and cylinder. The base of the cylindrical barrel, where it is attached to the cylinder, has a crowned “R”. The cylinder itself is decorated with a strand of small 6-pointed stars. On the left side of the revolver are the words "*Dassen Patent, Guss Stahl*".

1df2efa8-09f6-56fe-b40d-5cff853bf496.keywords: Revolver; solid frame; chamber cylinder; ejector; grip plates; checking; barrel; arms; armours; metalwork; war; warfare; military objects

1e2be9c1-6927-592d-9052-ed69ed5754c4.name: Ten piasters
1e2be9c1-6927-592d-9052-ed69ed5754c4.description: On obverse: "*amara bi ta'amul al-husayn bin 'ali 1338 'abduhu wa-ibn 'abdihi*" ("It is ordered to deal with by al-Hussein bin' Ali 1334, God servant"). On reverse: "*duriba bi-makka al-mukarrama sana 8 / al-hukuma al-'arabiyya al-hashimiyya / 'ashara / hashimi / qurush*" ("10 Piaster of Arab Hashemite Government, minted at Mecca al Mukarrama in reign year 8").

1f3e2539-13d7-58c9-871e-2d7832ae9523.name: Child among balls of yarn
1f3e2539-13d7-58c9-871e-2d7832ae9523.description2: In 1930, France imported nearly 350,000 tons of cotton, 2/3 of which came from the United States, with the rest coming from the British Iles and Egypt. The French cotton industry employed around 200,000 people at this time, mainly in the east and the north of the country.

1ff4925b-b991-516d-9e19-a6960fbbbed1.name: *Marseille, view of the maritime port*
1ff4925b-b991-516d-9e19-a6960fbbbed1.description2: Marseille port meant that overtook Le Havre in terms of importance in the mid 19th century, as it became the first French port - and one of the largest international ports - to transport both people and goods. As the old harbour was not big enough to accommodate the growing number of ships and their increasingly important cargo new harbours were built, such as that in La Joliette.

20b75da3-3556-540c-a1f6-b0db4ca7d41f.name: A view of London
20b75da3-3556-540c-a1f6-b0db4ca7d41f.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
20b75da3-3556-540c-a1f6-b0db4ca7d41f.keywords: London; Buildings; Cathedrals; Streets; St Paul's Cathedral; Cityscapes; stereoscopic photography; stereoscope; stereograph
20b75da3-3556-540c-a1f6-b0db4ca7d41f.description2:
A stereograph is a pair of photographic images of the same subject taken from slightly different angles. This gives the illusion of a single three-dimensional image when viewed through a stereoscope designed to hold it. Stereographs were mass produced. Viewing them was a popular amusement carried out in the home from the 1850s until the early 20th century.  
This stereograph is from a series entitled 'Instantaneous Views of London'. The word 'instantaneous' reveals that an important selling-point for such photographs was that they quickly captured a moment in time. In this case the crowd and carriages of a busy London street are frozen in motion.

2186b4e6-4e67-5ef6-a1b9-1f095be746ab.name: Reconstruction of a late AH 13th – early 14th century / AD 19th – early 20th-century trading vessel
2186b4e6-4e67-5ef6-a1b9-1f095be746ab.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
2186b4e6-4e67-5ef6-a1b9-1f095be746ab.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
2186b4e6-4e67-5ef6-a1b9-1f095be746ab.description2: This reconstruction of a *baghla* was commissioned by His Highness Dr Shaikh Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi in 2004 to represent the most important and largest type of trading craft that plied the waters between the Gulf and India in the late 13th/ 19th century and the early 14th/ 20th century. Built by Emirati and Omani specialists, the vessel incorporates all the traditional elements of a baghla: a length of around 30 meters, two masts for lateen sails, its typically parrot-shaped stem head, its high square stern and its lavishly carved design. All these features were originally influenced by the design of Portuguese ships.

22722c3a-12c3-54d0-9366-27dfa3fd737f.name: Banknote
22722c3a-12c3-54d0-9366-27dfa3fd737f.keywords: Egyptian currency; money minting; coin; paper money; Abbas Helmy II
22722c3a-12c3-54d0-9366-27dfa3fd737f.description2: 50 piasters from the days of Khedive `Abbas Hilmi II. During this time, a collection of Ottoman coins made of silver and copper circulated, valued at one, five and ten piasters. They were minted in AH 1327 / AD 1909 and bore the name of the Ottoman Sultan Muhammad V. However, the most important monetary event took place in 1898, when Khedive `Abbas Hilmi II granted a franchise to Raphael Suares to establish the National Bank of Egypt. This franchise gave him the right to produce securities that were accepted to pay domanial money, and the right to cash this money as gold upon demand.

229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.name: Beirut Railway Station
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.description: This railway station, built during the Ottoman period, was the first railway station in Lebanon. It was a public station, intended for both for the transportation of passengers and trading goods.
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.history: The Beirut-Damascus railway line, opened in 1895, was built across mountainous terrain to a 1,050 mm gauge. The second line from Riyaq to Aleppo, via Lebanon's eastern Beqaa valley, was also approved around this time. This was built to a standard gauge, even though it was only intended to provide a service between Damascus and Aleppo. The northern city of Tripoli was also connected via railway to Homs.
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.keywords: Commerce; Train station; Railway; Transportation; Trading
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.architects: “Société des chemins de fer Ottomans économique de Beyrouth-damas-Hauran”

24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.name: Flag
24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.author: Huda Kilani
24e0347f-f9f3-5254-ba16-aef618e16ba6.description2: A piece of green Syrian silk fabric, inset on the top of the mast, which used to be carried during religious ceremonies. Trade and crafts were common activities in Jordan between the late 19th century and the earlier 20th century. These activities depended on migration and attracted groups of people who travelled or settled in the Jordanian territory to produce or sell products. Thus, the exchange of goods among different areas was very common, as exemplified by this object and many traditional dresses. Silk textiles were very common products in the Jordanian and Palestinian areas and were purchased from Syria, being an element in local fashion, both in Jordan and in Palestine.

2550c1a6-5124-5e2b-bba4-a5c2f062b159.name: The port of Aqaba

257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.name: Postcard of Khan Antoun Bey Square
257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.keywords: Postcard; Khan; Souk; Trade; Economy; Beirut
257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.description2: Located next to the port, the Khan Antoun Bey Square was the entrance to the city for those arriving by sea. By the 19th century the *khan* itself, pictured here, housed trading offices on the ground and first floors and foreign consulates on the upper floors. The inner courtyard was used to park the consuls' horse-drawn carriages.

2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.name: Outline map of Damascus in 1918
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.author: Stefan Weber
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.second_name: Indicating urban growth to the fin de siecle
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.description2: Damascus, now the political and cultural centre of Syria, is one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities. The design of its living spaces and the organization of urban society were always connected to the culture of its inhabitants. Damascus’ geographical space reflects this “spatial turn”: Its public spaces were clearly shaped and influenced by the diverse social, historical and cultural structures and events, which contributed to the vitality of Damascus’ multilayered Urban Design.

27238194-345e-5c00-b880-860d50c950cf.name: The trademark for Chocolat des Pyramides produced by the company Talmone, based in Turin (Italy)
27238194-345e-5c00-b880-860d50c950cf.author: Margherita Martelli
27238194-345e-5c00-b880-860d50c950cf.archival: ACS, Ministero dell’Industria, del Commercio e dell’Artigianato, Ufficio Italiano Brevetti e Marchi, Serie Marchi, Fasc. 284
27238194-345e-5c00-b880-860d50c950cf.third_name: *Chocolat des Pyramides*, cioccolato, Ditta Michele Talmone, Torino
27238194-345e-5c00-b880-860d50c950cf.description2: The Talmone chocolate factory was founded in Turin in 1850. In 1929 merged with Venchi.

272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.name: Brass head of flagpole
272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.author: Huda Kilani
272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.description2: This mast, made of casted brass, bears an Arabic calligraphic decoration with the inscription "Oh God, Oh Muhammad". It is fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

274e910c-7ec1-5f20-8460-292341da7d08.name: Headdress
274e910c-7ec1-5f20-8460-292341da7d08.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
274e910c-7ec1-5f20-8460-292341da7d08.author: Huda Kilani
274e910c-7ec1-5f20-8460-292341da7d08.keywords: silver chains; coins; decorated; Ottoman coins; Venice coins
274e910c-7ec1-5f20-8460-292341da7d08.description2: Three silver chains formed into a hat with beaded frontispiece decorated with coins. On the back, a long fabric with gold and silver Ottoman and Venice coins. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for these purposes. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.name: Yıldız Tile Imperial Factory
275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; Ancient Istanbul; yıldız tile; ceramic; factories
275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.description2: The Yıldız Tile Imperial Factory was founded by Sultan Abdülhamid II (1876-1909) in the early 1890’s in the garden of Yıldız Palace for the purposes of arousing, reshaping and stimulating the Turkish tiling art. The factory, which began manufacturing immediately, was damaged in the earthquake of 1894 and in the same year, it was nearly reconstructed by Italian Architect Raimondo d’Aronco.

281a9738-8bd7-5011-a3f4-2866ccff808e.name: Official document regarding the inauguration of the Beirut–Damascus railway
281a9738-8bd7-5011-a3f4-2866ccff808e.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
281a9738-8bd7-5011-a3f4-2866ccff808e.description2: This document records the inauguration of the Ottoman Beirut-Damascus-Hawran railway company, headed by Hasan Effendi Bayham.

28a47b67-f1e7-5f4c-8ee1-b205470d3b94.name: For the working classes. All sorts of good available to buy on credit, paying 1 franc a week.
28a47b67-f1e7-5f4c-8ee1-b205470d3b94.description2: As the working class expanded to huge numbers due to industrial developments and rural exodus to the cities, they also became an important pawn in the nation's economic game. Banks and businesses  introduced systems of paying by credit, claiming to help the less privileged. This poster, for examples, claims that a simple credit system would allow this family to radically change their life, affording them a larger and better lit home, nicer clothes, and a more luxurious dinner on the table.

28ad9737-7a52-5383-8f8a-2a5177cead7c.name: Bookmark
28ad9737-7a52-5383-8f8a-2a5177cead7c.holder: The House of Antique Tin Boxes

28ad9737-7a52-5383-8f8a-2a5177cead7c.keywords: Esposizione Internazionale di Torino; trade; trademark; commerce; Italian firms; nationalism; raw material; finished product; Egypt; exoticism; popular culture; Italians in Egypt
28ad9737-7a52-5383-8f8a-2a5177cead7c.description2: Gadget having scimitar shape distributed by a Company producing Talmone Chocolate and presented during the International Exhibition of Turin in 1911. The bookmark is part of an advertising using an Egyptian exotic style, which was very common in those years.
28ad9737-7a52-5383-8f8a-2a5177cead7c.holding_institution_org: La Casa delle Antiche Scatole di Latta

28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.name: North African caravan, in the west of the Sahara
28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.third_name: A Travers le Monde, Paris: Hachette, 1895–1914
28f6f7de-3daa-59e6-960d-f0cac66b210d.description2: Camille Douls (1864–1889), who was passionate  about Africa, decided in the late 19th century to enter indigenous North African territory, despite it being forbidden for foreigners at the time. He began to learn Arabic and study the Quran for this purpose, and was able to live among the Oulad Delim tribe for five months, although not without risk to his personal safety. He published his observations on his return (1888), which attracted much attention, as no European had lived among these people to date. He was assassinated the following year during a trip to Algeria. The tale of his time in the desert was illustrated by Jules Girardet, an artist specialising in historical scenes who had never seen the subjects of his drawings. This image is therefore interesting, as it sheds light on the nature of the stereotypical Western gaze on nomadic lifestyles.

2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.name: *The Bazaar at Athens*
2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.author: Tsigakou 1995, 114, fig. 6
2aa49918-c570-5090-b9c9-670c7ca75ff7.description2: The well-known Irish topographer Edward Dodwell toured Greece twice: in 1801 and 1805–6 and he later produced several works on Greece’s scenery, its antiquities and the people’s life. He managed to cover a wide range of Greek subjects and to record faithfully-in both his drawings and his descriptions- various aspects of Greek life and customs. Dodwell’s folio *Views in Greece* (1821) includes an identical image entitled “Bazaar of Athens”, which is obviously based on this watercolour. According to the artist’s description in the text, on the right-hand side is seen a coffee-shop frequented by important people, such as the disdar (e.g. Governor of Athens) depicted in a scarlet gown.

en: Tsigakou, Fani-Maria, *British Images of Greece from the Benaki Museum Collections*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1995.

2b300ed4-450b-52f6-8868-c8f548313061.description: Half piaster: On obverse: "*al-husayn / bin 'ali / 'abduhu / wa-ibn 'abdihi / wafqa Allah*" ("Hussein bin Ali God Servant and son of God Servant Granted by God"). 2e9bb9ef-0628-53b2-88c7-0bb1e2984d88.description: A bronze mint-mould holding six coins, in use at the mint in Fez during the reign of Sultan Mulay al-Hasan I (r. 1873-94). It should be noted that, compared to earlier periods, coinage was evolving quickly in relation to industry at this time.

2ea1c843-e974-5276-8455-c507ef6d058b.name: The Algerian Tailor [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
2ea1c843-e974-5276-8455-c507ef6d058b.author: Marina Minozzi
2ea1c843-e974-5276-8455-c507ef6d058b.archival: *L'Esposizione di Parigi del 1878 illustrata*, Sonzogno Editore, 1878, p. 145
2ea1c843-e974-5276-8455-c507ef6d058b.keywords: Exposition universelle de Paris; industrialisation; exhibition building; Moorish city; exhibitions and urban spaces; Moorish style; Islamic architecture; reinterpretation; exoticism; reproduction; model; magazine

2ea1c843-e974-5276-8455-c507ef6d058b.description2: At the International Exhibition in Paris, 1878, commercial activities typical of the colony were performed in the park next to Trocadero Pavilion, as part of the reconstruction of a hypothetical typical neighbourhood. The character shown here is an Algerian tailor.

2fd7dbb0-f684-52f4-93f3-b485ecf82f5e.name: Postcard: *The Strait of Gibraltar in the Future*
2fd7dbb0-f684-52f4-93f3-b485ecf82f5e.description: This curious postcard with a utopian vision of how the Strait of Gibraltar could become in the future was sent to the Marquis of Cerralbo by a friend, Gabriel Vich, but never received a stamp. Although it shows the address of the marquis, maybe it was posted inside an envelope or delivered, finally, on hand. This kind of ephemera was published by the fortnightly publication España en África (Spain in Africa), active in the first decades of the 20th century. The image represented is a beautiful commercial and geopolitical project that would have linked two continents with a 15 km bridge.
2fd7dbb0-f684-52f4-93f3-b485ecf82f5e.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes
2fd7dbb0-f684-52f4-93f3-b485ecf82f5e.third_name: Tarjeta postal: *El Estrecho de Gibrlatar en el porvenir*

3018b07a-449e-5452-bb78-bbcfe4a57bdc.name: Beirut Port Train Station
3018b07a-449e-5452-bb78-bbcfe4a57bdc.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Rita El Hachem
3018b07a-449e-5452-bb78-bbcfe4a57bdc.description2: This station was used to deliver supplies from Beirut port to the main train station in Beirut, located in Mar Mikhael. The station was an important addition to the region's trade system, linking the sea routes the land routes.

309c53a9-a0ef-5547-8426-cd89d2b38012.name: Istanbul Port
309c53a9-a0ef-5547-8426-cd89d2b38012.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
309c53a9-a0ef-5547-8426-cd89d2b38012.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; Ancient Istanbul; Port; Trade
309c53a9-a0ef-5547-8426-cd89d2b38012.description2: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. The construction of Galata Pier began in 1892, and was completed in 1900. Two warehouses were built in 1910, and three more were added in 1928. From 1925 on, the port authority started to give all the necessary logistics support to the ships, including water and coal supply, loading and unloading, maritime pilotage and marine salvage services.

30b8ffa8-c9e2-5376-85c7-4955c327cf33.name: Bracelet
30b8ffa8-c9e2-5376-85c7-4955c327cf33.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
30b8ffa8-c9e2-5376-85c7-4955c327cf33.author: Huda Kilani
30b8ffa8-c9e2-5376-85c7-4955c327cf33.description2: Niello made by a Circassian silver smith. Mounted with an oval-shaped piece, with locking mechanism, decorated with niello decoration. The immigration of the Circassians to the Eastern Arab countries (they have spiritual and religious links with these countries) started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900.

30b913ab-d3b2-56b2-ac63-f81083c8e870.name: Theresian thaler
30b913ab-d3b2-56b2-ac63-f81083c8e870.keywords: Arabian Pensinsula; Maria Theresia; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics
30b913ab-d3b2-56b2-ac63-f81083c8e870.description2: The Maria Theresian Thaler, a large silver coin originally created by Queen (Empress) Maria Theresia, minted in Austria until 1890. It was used in the Arabic Peninsula as a means of payment. This coin was countersigned at the Arabian mint of Ras Bab el Mandeb in 1890.

31ecc09c-c7d7-5ac6-a176-853bf5723059.name: Five piasters
31ecc09c-c7d7-5ac6-a176-853bf5723059.description: Ottoman AR-5 qurush minted at Constantinople in AH 1327 / AD 1909. On obverse: within border of 24 stars and 12 crescents, *tuğra* of sultan Muhammad V, "Rashad" to the right, "reign year 1" below. On reverse: within border of 24 stars and 12 crescents, "*\`azza nasruhu duriba fi al-qustantiniyya 1327*" ("May his victory be glorious struck in Constantinople, 1327").
