3322889b-90a0-56de-acf0-715553f9bb35.name: Map of Beirut as it appeared in 1841
3322889b-90a0-56de-acf0-715553f9bb35.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
3322889b-90a0-56de-acf0-715553f9bb35.keywords: Beirut; Mediterranean; Ancient harbour; Coastal geomorphology; Port; Coastline
3322889b-90a0-56de-acf0-715553f9bb35.description2: This map shows Beirut before construction works were taken to modernise the harbour. The coastline has changed significantly since then.

341be9d6-6bac-5978-aa0e-844e03633f92.name: The port of Brăila
341be9d6-6bac-5978-aa0e-844e03633f92.archival: *Donau-Album. Malerische Reise von Regensburg bis Sulina. Album du Danube. Voyage pittoresque de Ratisbonne a Souline. Danube Album. A picturesque travel from Ratisbon to Suline. A Duna. Festöi utazas Regensburg-tol a Sulina torkolatig*, Vienna, A. Hartleben, 1880
341be9d6-6bac-5978-aa0e-844e03633f92.description2: In 1829, an annex to the peace treaty of Edirne, that was concluded after the Russo-Ottoman war of 1828-1829, concerned the Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia. One of its provisions was that the Sublime Porte had to give back to Wallachia the three cities situated on the left bank of the Danube, which it had conquered in the 15h-16th centuries. Among these was Brăila, a port on the Danube annexed by the Ottomans at around 1540. After 1829 measures were taken by the local authorities for the modernization of Brăila. The port subsequently developed thanks to the growth of Wallachian commerce as a consequence of the fact that by the treaty of Edirne the Ottoman Empire granted the freedom of commerce to the Romanian Principalities. In 1838 Brăila was given the status of free port (with no or few customs duties).

348c2a80-0242-562a-93bb-7572f6c98b1b.name: Map of Beirut port
348c2a80-0242-562a-93bb-7572f6c98b1b.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
348c2a80-0242-562a-93bb-7572f6c98b1b.description2: This map shows Beirut port after its expansion in 1890.

351cda3e-2855-5288-9f93-722ee2410530.name: Beykoz Pavilion
351cda3e-2855-5288-9f93-722ee2410530.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
351cda3e-2855-5288-9f93-722ee2410530.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; Ancient Istanbul; pavilion
351cda3e-2855-5288-9f93-722ee2410530.description2: The construction of Beykoz Pavilion began by order of Mehmed Ali Pahsa, Governor of Egypt in 1845 and upon his death was completed in 1854. The two-storeyed, half-timbered building has a symmetrical plan and neo-classical façade and designed as a hall in the middle with rooms surrounded. Photographs of the pavilion taken during the reign of Sultan Abdülhamid II reveal its rich decoration with gilded furniture, upholsteries and curtains of Hereke fabrics, Baccarat vases and large crystal chandeliers.

351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.name: Au Palais Arabe. A furniture shop of the Italians Eugenio and Alfredo Coen in Tunis
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th–early 20th century
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.author: Giulia Barrera
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 164
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.description2: “Au Palais Arabe”, Rue de Rome, 3, Tunis, was once the most important shop in town for furniture and other household items. Eugenio Coen (born in Livorno in 1855, migrated to Tunis in 1885) and his brother Alfredo (born in Livorno in 1868 and migrated to Tunis in 1887) also ran a furniture factory that, in 1906, employed about 100 carpenters, cabinet makers and other workers, 80 per cent of whom were Italian.

37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.name: Tool to open oysters
37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.type: Wood and iron knife to open oysters
37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.dimensions: Length c. 185 mm, overall width c. 25 mm
37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
37f2def9-cf7f-5ab5-b473-ee0a55d36f21.description2: This simple implement is an oyster-shucking knife, known as miflaqa (pl. mafaliq).  Such implements are already mentioned in historical sources, including the writings of Al-Idrisi and Ibn Battuta. However, in those days, they were associated with separating and freeing the oysters from the seabed. In more recent times, tools such as this one were definitely used to open the pearl oysters.

3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.name: Egyptian Furniture of the Italian Giuseppe Parvis Living in Cairo [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.author: Marina Minozzi
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.archival: *L'Esposizione di Parigi del 1878 illustrata*, Sonzogno Editore, 1878, p. 632.
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.keywords: International exhibition; universal exposition; Exposition universelle de Paris; pavillion; social change; applied arts; model; Moorish style; house; middle class; market; trade; Italian craftsmanship; Italians in Egypt; artistic exchange
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.copyright: Copyright image: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma.
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.third_name: *Mobili egiziani del'italiano Giuseppe Parvis dimorante al Cairo*
3854487a-c60c-5835-adc0-fa6fe0ed8d59.description2: Giuseppe Parvis, who emigrated from Italy to Egypt, began extensive production of elegant furniture adapted to Arabian taste and decorated with mother-of-pearl and metal inserts. He won awards for his work at the Universal Exhibitions of Paris in 1867, Vienna and Philadelphia. Giuseppe Parvis is an example of successful businessman who successfully adapted to the Egyptian market. He was able to run laboratories with 50 workers and trained a large number of students in ebony furniture making. Over the span of 20 years he introduced and sold furniture to Arabian people who traditionally did not possess such furniture, using an Arabic style and taste and by using woods found in the East, Egypt and China.

387152c3-f2e6-5090-9494-72805f950568.name: AUB Tramway
387152c3-f2e6-5090-9494-72805f950568.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Rita El Hachem
387152c3-f2e6-5090-9494-72805f950568.description2: The Beirut tramway, which covered a total of 12 kilometres in the city's centre, was opened in April 1908, during the Ottoman era. It was used all through the French Mandate era and was finally closed in September 1965.

3a2530bf-22b3-5651-bacc-f8a748c678a1.name: Headdress
3a2530bf-22b3-5651-bacc-f8a748c678a1.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
3a2530bf-22b3-5651-bacc-f8a748c678a1.author: Huda Kilani
3a2530bf-22b3-5651-bacc-f8a748c678a1.keywords: cotton; embroidered; gold coins; Ottoman coins
3a2530bf-22b3-5651-bacc-f8a748c678a1.materials: Gold, silver, cotton fabric, silk; casting; hand embroidered
3a2530bf-22b3-5651-bacc-f8a748c678a1.description2: A rectangular piece of cotton cloth embroidered with cross-stitching forming a bonnet with a line of 70 gold coins (*ghawasi*) sewn together on the front, with two pieces of cloth on the top sides with silver Ottoman coins and red stuffed velvet pursed from the back side with 7 silver Ottoman coins. The silver coins were used as money and as jewellery given by the groom to the bride, thus being an indication of his financial status. This object reflects the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It illustrates common elements and traditions in the area in fashion, costumes and social rites. There were no political boundaries at that period between the Jordanian and Palestinians territories. Some cities were like twins because of their close proximity and the exchange of trade goods and business.

3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.name: The Ottoman Bank
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph bank; economy
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.description2: One of the world's largest photo archives, Abdülhamid II's photo archives – knows as the Yildiz Albums – contain about 37 thousand pictures from that period of the Ottoman Empire. The photo archives contain images of cities, buildings which were built by sultan, schools, students, soldiers, mosques, ports, government departments, shipyards, railways, bridges, bazaars, machines, locomotives and factories. The Ottoman Bank was founded in 1856 in the Galata business section of Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire, as a joint venture between British interests, the Banque de Paris et des Pays-Bas of France, and the Ottoman government. *Tanzimat* era's principal renovations in the financial field were the reestablishment of the currency and the foundation of the Ottoman Bank.

3c0de00c-d143-5139-b9fd-ae28536aadec.name: Map of the Beirut–Damascus railway
3c0de00c-d143-5139-b9fd-ae28536aadec.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
3c0de00c-d143-5139-b9fd-ae28536aadec.description2: This map shows the railway line connecting Beirut and Damascus. The table on the right shows the distance between each city along horse tracks.

3cd68daa-dde5-568b-8623-dcdb17c2cf59.name: One piaster/Type 2
3cd68daa-dde5-568b-8623-dcdb17c2cf59.author: Aida Naghawi
3cd68daa-dde5-568b-8623-dcdb17c2cf59.keywords: Hussein bin Ali; ten piasters; Arab Hashemite Government; Mecca al Mukarrama; coin; currency; coinage; numismatics
3cd68daa-dde5-568b-8623-dcdb17c2cf59.description2: One piaster (type 2), bronze. On obverse, in the middle within a circle of dots, “*al-husayn bin ‘ali*” (“al-Hussein bin ‘Ali”). Marginal legend: “*amara bi-ta‘amul ‘abduhu wa-ibn ‘abdihi / sana 8*” (“It is orders to deal with, God’s Servant and son of God’s Servant, Year 8”). On reverse, in middle within a circle of dots: “*duriba bi-makka al-mukarrama 1334*” (“Minted at Makka al-Mukarrama 1334”). Marginal Legend: “*al-hukuma al-‘arabiyya al-hashimiyya qurush wahid raqam 1 bi-dakhili murabba\`*” (“Arab Hashemite Government, one piaster and number 1 is a square”).

3d414881-32eb-5cec-9499-511e26749367.name: Photograph of Bab al-Saraya
3d414881-32eb-5cec-9499-511e26749367.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
3d414881-32eb-5cec-9499-511e26749367.description2: Bab al-Saraya was the eastern gate of the city. Whilst other gates were closed at dusk, this was the only gate that was kept open until evening prayer. Thus, it was also commonly known as *bab al-masla*, meaning the worshipper's gate. The official name, Bab al-Saraya, comes from its proximity to the Serail of the Amir Fakhr al-Din by the Sursuq market. It was also located near the Amir Mansur Assaf mosque on the sea front. The gate remained intact until it was destroyed by the French authorities during the mandate era, in 1927. The headquarters of an-Nahar, a famous Lebanese newspaper, now occupy the site.

3f4c6fa9-1eb4-5cf8-b351-d019a0e81489.name: Robert Hamilton Lang
3f4c6fa9-1eb4-5cf8-b351-d019a0e81489.description2: Lang was manager of the Imperial Ottoman Bank in Larnaka, 1863–1872, that ran the finances of the Ottoman administration. He conducted excavations at Dali (ancient Idlaion) in the centre of the island in the late 1860s. His report is the first systematic account of an excavation produced on the island. Lang went on to a series of posts with the IOB in Alexandria, Romania and Constantinople, becoming Director General of the bank. He was honoured by Queen Victoria, the king of Rumania, the Khedive and the Sultan.

412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.name: Jars from the Company of Glass and Mosaic of Venice and Murano [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.author: Marina Minozzi
412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.archival: *L'Esposizione di Parigi del 1878 illustrata*, Sonzogno Editore, 1878, p. 340.
412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.keywords: Applied arts; minor arts; manufacture; craftsmanship; museums of applied arts; model; reproduction; decoration; motifs; collection; collector; glass; Murano glass; glasswork; Venice; Salviati; book; International exhibitions; market; trade
412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.copyright: Copyright image: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma.
412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.third_name: *Vasi della Compagnia di Vetri e Mosaici di Venezia e Murano*
412af98f-597f-5bd8-9bce-18aac056c045.description2: “The Chronicle of the Universal Exhibition of Paris” of 1878 celebrates the city of Murano’s commercial success in glass production. A large number of these objects reside in the collection of the Museum of Industrial Arts in Rome (M.A.I.), now part of the acquisitions of the National Museum of Antique Art on display at Palazzo Barberini. M.A.I. was established in 1872 in Rome as a collection of manufacts (glasses, majolica, sculptures, materials, photographs, metals, casts and other) from antiquity to 19th century, and as a training school for specialising artisans, as part of the process of revaluation of the so-called "minor arts". Venetian glass has a long history, inherited from the Roman, Byzantine and Islamic tradition in the Middle Ages. These jars were manufactured by the famous glass company Salviati, founded in 1866 and established in Venice and Murano. In presenting these objects they claimed the rebirth of a long-forgotten antique art and the rebirth of glass industries in Italy. Tomb excavations brought to light a series of vases. New objects based on those excavated were made on the occasion of the International Exhibition in Paris in 1878.

43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.name: The Pearl Carpet
43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.materials: Pearls, silk, deer hide, beads, gems
43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.description2: The foundation of silk and fine deer hide is densely embroidered overall with a design worked in strings of natural ‘Basra’ pearls, measuring approximately 1-3 mm, and English coloured glass beads. There are on average 78 pearls and beads per vertical dm. (10 cm), and 68 per horizontal dm., equaling a density of c.4,990 pearls and beads per dm2. The total area of the carpet is c. 45,670 cm2. The 32 smaller rosettes cover an area of c. 400 cm2 with smaller gems, and the total area embroidered with pearls and is beads is approximately 44,500 cm2. Therefore, over 2.2 million pearls and beads have been used to decorate the field. In our estimation, the number of pearls employed in the design is therefor at least 1.2-1.5 million.

4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.name: Pearl Diver’s Nose Clip
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.type: Horn pearl diver's nose clip on cotton string
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.dimensions: Length of the horn nose clip c. 60 mm
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.keywords: futam, aftama; khubat; libas al-ghawas; dyyin
4454c9bf-8d06-539a-b793-d2ce0b56e6f8.description2: This simple, but effective nose clip, known as futam (pl. aftama) in the Gulf region, was traditionally made of horn, wood or occasionally tortoise shell. Historical sources reaching back to the 4th century H/ 10th century AD already describe the clips' distinctive 'arrow' or 'scissor' shape, which remained largely unchanged until modern times. Equipped only with his noseclip, finger guards (khubat), occasionally a protective suit against jelly fish (libas al-ghaws) and a basket or bag (dyyin) for the oysters, a pearl diver would descend 50-60 times every day to bring up as many oysters as he could.

4543ccbf-dceb-5300-941b-8c2f10ba3b29.name: The port of Galaţi
4543ccbf-dceb-5300-941b-8c2f10ba3b29.description2: After the Russian annexation of Bessarabia (the eastern part of Moldavia) in 1812 and until the restoration by Russia of Southern Bessarabia (1856), Galați remained Moldavia’s only port on the Danube. Understanding the city’s importance for Moldavia’s economy and wanting to ensure its development, prince Mihail Sturdza, who was appointed ruler of Moldavia by the Sublime Porte in 1834, issued in 1836 an act stipulating that Galați was to be a free port (with no or few customs duties) starting with March 1837. Also, a new neighborhood was to be built based on modern urban planning prescriptions and Galați received the right to organize annually five national fairs, during which traders from everywhere could sell any type of products.

46069753-8d25-527b-8ca3-f62f78f6b3d2.name: Algerian Shoemaker at the Trocadéro [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
46069753-8d25-527b-8ca3-f62f78f6b3d2.author: Marina Minozzi
46069753-8d25-527b-8ca3-f62f78f6b3d2.archival: *L'Esposizione di Parigi del 1878 illustrata*, Sonzogno Editore, 1878, p. 108
46069753-8d25-527b-8ca3-f62f78f6b3d2.keywords: Exposition universelle de Paris; industrialisation; exhibition building; Moorish city; exhibitions and urban spaces; Moorish style; Islamic architecture; reinterpretation; exoticism; reproduction; model; magazine
46069753-8d25-527b-8ca3-f62f78f6b3d2.copyright: Copyright image: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma.
46069753-8d25-527b-8ca3-f62f78f6b3d2.description2: At the International Exhibition in Paris, 1878, commercial activities typical of the colony were performed in the park next to Trocadero Pavilion, as part of the reconstruction of a hypothetical typical neighbourhood. The characters shown here are Algerian shoemakers from the Trocadero area working under a tent.

4620f58e-dafe-517f-be48-e848bac5e3df.name: Coin
4620f58e-dafe-517f-be48-e848bac5e3df.keywords: Egyptian currency; money minting; coin; paper money; Sultan Hussein Kamel
4620f58e-dafe-517f-be48-e848bac5e3df.description2: Samples of the money used during the reign of Sultan Husayn Kamil. Egyptian money bore the names of Ottoman sultans until World War I, when Egypt ceased to be part of the Ottoman Empire, and was declared a Sultanate under British protection. Money, at the time of Sultan Husayn Kamil, was minted in British mints. Coins circulated at the time of Sultan Husayn Kamil are considered special as they bore his name in the form of “Sultan Husayn Kamil” and the date of his accession to the throne (AH 1333 / AD 1914). Thus, Egyptian money bore no sign of subservience to the Ottoman Empire. During the days of Sultan Husayn Kamil, gold coins were minted as golden 100 piasters; silver two, five, and 20 piasters; and nickel one and five dimes.

4680c1d7-2d7f-504c-983e-43f220f6f53b.name: One piaster
4680c1d7-2d7f-504c-983e-43f220f6f53b.description: One piaster ( type 1), bronze. On obverse: "*al-husayn / bin 'ali / 'abduhu / wa-ibn 'abdihi / wafqa Allah*" ("Hussein bin Ali God Servant and son of God Servant Granted by God"). On reverse: "*duriba sana 1334 sana 5 / makka al-mukarrama / 'asima al-hukuma / al-'arabiyya al-hashimiyya / qurush wahid*" ("One piaster minted in 1334 /reign year 5 at Makka al-Mukarrama capital of Hashemite Arab Government").
4680c1d7-2d7f-504c-983e-43f220f6f53b.author: Aida Naghawi
4680c1d7-2d7f-504c-983e-43f220f6f53b.keywords: Hussein bin Ali; one piaster; Arab Hashemite Government; Mecca al Mukarrama; coin; currency; coinage; numismatics

46e5760e-4ca7-5891-b293-149dd73cdb25.name: *View of Jaffa*
46e5760e-4ca7-5891-b293-149dd73cdb25.description: Travel illustrations in the 19th century, with their images of life, history and topography, had a great influence over Orientalism. This engraving appeared in a publication about the history of Turkey. Jaffa was a very important port in East Mediterranean.
46e5760e-4ca7-5891-b293-149dd73cdb25.author: Carmen Linés Viñuales

48830cf5-a66b-5e0d-b2f1-e3106f154a03.name: 50 Piastres
48830cf5-a66b-5e0d-b2f1-e3106f154a03.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
48830cf5-a66b-5e0d-b2f1-e3106f154a03.keywords: Commerce; trade; Currency; Coins; coinage; Numismatics
48830cf5-a66b-5e0d-b2f1-e3106f154a03.description2: This 50 piastres bank note bears no watermark.

48bd5c22-4c67-599d-a92c-16a8ba8b932a.name: Moroccan coins
48bd5c22-4c67-599d-a92c-16a8ba8b932a.description: Coin struck in 1903 under Mulay Sultan ‘Abd al-‘Aziz al-Hasan I (r. 1894 to 1908) at the mint in Fez. For a century (1800-1900) the ‘Alawid sultans struck coins in the workshops of Fez, but due to the economic crisis at the time, gold was unavailable so most coins were of silver, bronze or other common metals – although the technique remained the same, with the metal poured into moulds. The patterns on the face and on the back vary between the star with eight points (Solomon ring) and the indication of the place of mint.
48bd5c22-4c67-599d-a92c-16a8ba8b932a.holder: Numismatic Museum of the al-Maghreb Bank
48bd5c22-4c67-599d-a92c-16a8ba8b932a.keywords: Coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; gold; silver; bronze; mint; moulding; moulds; six-pointed star; ring; workshop; traditional coinage; European influence

4b719ab5-caa8-53d7-a185-809f12af918c.name: Venetian mirror
4b719ab5-caa8-53d7-a185-809f12af918c.holder: Musée d’Histoire Moderne et Contemporaine de Kassar Saïd
4b719ab5-caa8-53d7-a185-809f12af918c.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
4b719ab5-caa8-53d7-a185-809f12af918c.description2: This magnificent wooden mirror, carved and decorated with gold leaf, is deeply moulded (14cm) and engraved with floral patterns. Two different tones of gold leaf, matte and gloss, were used. This Italian style carving was very fashionable with the 19th century nobility.

4bef9a7e-ee5d-50e6-bbc2-ad9258836fd3.name: Carlo de Rossetti (consul of the Grand Duke of Tuscany) gives notice of a new ferry boat service between Alexandria (Egypt) and Constantinople operated by a Tuscan steamship
4bef9a7e-ee5d-50e6-bbc2-ad9258836fd3.author: Cristina Francioli
4bef9a7e-ee5d-50e6-bbc2-ad9258836fd3.archival: AS Li, Governo civile e militare, b. 890
4bef9a7e-ee5d-50e6-bbc2-ad9258836fd3.third_name: *Notificazione concernente l’attivazione di corse regolari fra Alessandria e Costantinopoli, e viceversa, mediante il Battello a Vapore Toscano* Il Generoso, *ed il suo servizio*
4bef9a7e-ee5d-50e6-bbc2-ad9258836fd3.description2: The steamboat Il Generoso had three classes of service: the first-class ticket cost 42.5 Thalers and the second class one 30 Thalers; they both included meals. By contrast, the third-class ticket (12 Thalers) did not entitle one to meals. The trip lasted five days. According to the poster, the steamboat Il Generoso was equipped with “very confortable cabins and living rooms, including a special living room for ladies”.

4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.name: Pearl Trader’s Scales Box
4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.description2: This wooden box was designed to contain a sophisticated scales set, which incorporated both a large balance and bowls for weighing quantities of pearls and a smaller version, with several, graded weighing bowls for smaller quantities. The weighing systems for pearls was complex and highly sophisticated to allow for the accurate assessment of mixed batches of pearls of varying sizes and quality. The largest and most valuable pearls were separated and assessed individually. The other pearls would be passed through graded sieves and separated into three batches of specific size.  Apart from the very best items, pearls from these batches were sold by weight.

4cb2c7b0-e6c5-5421-ba04-8e3b26cad183.name: Purse
4cb2c7b0-e6c5-5421-ba04-8e3b26cad183.description: Miser’s purses, also known as ring or string purses, were very popular feminine accessories during the 19th century and even the first decades of the following century. The Cerralbo Museum has a small collection of these kinds of pieces, souvenirs from Istanbul. This Turkish and colourful beadwork one, with its traditional geometric pattern and the promise of a fashionable outfit, would have surely delighted any lady.
4cb2c7b0-e6c5-5421-ba04-8e3b26cad183.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes

4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.name: Iron coffee roaster
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.author: Huda Kilani
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.keywords: coffee; coffee roasting; coffee beans; domestic furnishing
4d5b7131-33fe-5c5d-8076-ab9568f98e94.description2: Circular iron coffee roaster with long handle decorated with zigzag and triangle motifs. Coffee-drinking in a communal setting is an essential part of traditions in Bedouin communities to celebrate or mourn.

4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.name: Pearling Scales with their casing
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.type: Copper alloy and fibre pearling scales with metal and wood casing
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
4e0af093-1857-5b9b-90ef-f325bd3f29d4.description2: Pearling scales (mizan, pl. muwazin) like these were an essential tool for any pearl merchant as all aspects of a pearl’s physical appearance – its shape, hue, perfection, size and indeed weight - all determined its value and saleability. The scales typically consisted of small hemispherical copper alloy bowls suspended by simple string from a balance. Polished agate or - more rarely - copper alloy weights were used to determine the pearls' weights accurately. In order to prevent the scales from getting damaged, they were carefully stored in a purpose-made copper alloy container. The scales were generally made in India, with one known centre located in Ahmedabad.

4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.name: *Marketplace, Morocco*
4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
4e27b872-ecb5-5764-8ab4-12316b90ca21.description2: This imposing oil painting shows a caravan apparently leaving the gate of a North African city, perhaps Fez, with much commotion going on on either side of the camels and their guides. Although the title of the painting suggest a market scene, in reality little trading activity can be seen apart from an old hooded man sitting next to a large basket with shoes on the right. On the left a group of African men and a little child in a burnous admire the skills of a snake charmer, while his monkey next to him looks on intently. In the background, large numbers of men, apparently both of Arab and Berber origin, and dressed in a variety of traditional dress, walk along or stand together in groups conversing, oblivious to the camels, donkeys and horses moving inbetween them. Ferenc Eisenhut was an Austro-Hungarian painter, known for his monumentally conceived genre scenes of Eastern life and vistas. He was the only internationally acclaimed, Hungarian Orientalist painter.

51d89765-459f-5a2f-89bb-b09f35a3e9d2.name: Firman issued by Sultan Abdülmecid for the construction of the Constanţa–Cernavodă railway
51d89765-459f-5a2f-89bb-b09f35a3e9d2.description2: The first railway in the European part of the Ottoman Empire was built in Dobruja. Its construction was leased by the Ottoman sultan to the British company "Danube and Black Sea Railway and Kustendge harbour". According to the contract signed on 1 September 1857 the company had to build a railway linking the cities Constanţa and Cernavodă and could exploit it for 99 years, after which it became property of the Ottoman Empire. The railway, inaugurated on 4 October 1860, was 66 km long and was destined for freight transportation. After Dobruja was annexed by Romania in 1878, the state bought the railway from the British company (1882). Later, in order to connect it to the Romanian railway system (since Dobruja is separated from the rest of Romania by the Danube) a railway bridge was built across the Danube.

521421e0-80f1-5225-89de-67bdaec30210.name: Narrow street in Pera, Istanbul
521421e0-80f1-5225-89de-67bdaec30210.author: Maria Dimitriadou
521421e0-80f1-5225-89de-67bdaec30210.description2: A black and white photo from a leather bound album. It bepicts a narrow street in Pera, Constantinople, leading to the church of “Panagia tou Stavrodromiou”. Photographer unknown.

522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.name: Veil
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.author: Huda Kilani
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.keywords: Linen fabric; natural cotton; embroidered patterns
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.materials: Linen, silk; hand weaving, hand embroidered, natural dyes
522f2144-3034-5e4d-9bc3-6ef8c6f5ecd0.description2: Three natural cotton and linen fabrics sewn and decorated with cross-stitch with embroidered folkloric patterns (known as “cypress trees”, “amulets”, “keys”, “saw” and “Shuayb teeth”). They are mainly in red with some green colour; a small linen fringe dangles from two sides. The veil was an essential piece of women’s dress. Girls started preparing their trousseau (clothes, shawls, and other belongings collected for marriage) at the age of ten. Married women had various embroidered costumes worn for special occasions. As the economy of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th century-early 20th century relied on trades and crafts, new waves of traders and artisans started to arrive and to settle. Thus, traditional costumes reflect a variegated population composition, demographic changes, personal attire and local rites.

523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.name: An olive oil factory run by an Italian migrant in Monastir (Tunisia)
523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.author: Giulia Barrera
523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 217
523087c9-9a15-54a0-b37b-745c43c2cb51.description2: According to a 1895 survey by the Italian Chamber of Commerce of Tunisia, 82 modern olive-oil industries operated in the country; 34 (41 per cent) were run by Italians, 24 by French nationals, 19 by Tunisians and the remaining five by persons of other nationalities.

en: Finzi, Silvia (ed.), *Mestieri e professioni degli italiani di Tunisia/Métiers et professions des Italiens de Tunisie*, Tunis: Ambasciata d'Italia, Istituto di cultura, 2003.

5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.name: Kerosene lamp
5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.holder: Jordan Folklore Museum, Department of Antiquities
5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.author: Huda Kilani
5250886a-a6a0-5674-9156-a5f133b9cfe8.description2: A cylindrical container filled with gas and injected with air heats a group of emerging pipes from the cylinder, which are surrounded by glass to shield them from air and assist in hashing its light into place. Kerosene lamps were used to light the streets of Amman until the first electricity generator began to operate. The beginning of the 20th century marked the re-urbanisation of Amman after 500 years of abandonment.

52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.name: Amulet
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.type: Cultic Object; ornament; talismanic object; jewellery
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.author: Huda Kilani
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.keywords: Talisman; crescent; tusks; wild boar; heal of Gazalle
52bc1f5c-19f1-5c15-8794-630ecd367289.description2: This object is a piece of horse jewellery, an amulet worn around the horse's neck to ward off misfortune. Horse jewellery was used among Bedouins and villagers communities. This amulet consists of a silver-cased crescent composed of two joined tusks of wild boar. A ¼ Majidi Ottoman gold coin dangles from the crescent with three crescents and stars at the end. The silver chain is called “heal of gazelle”.

5381cedb-dcaf-5b98-864b-12a4d739c029.name: State Bank of Morocco
5381cedb-dcaf-5b98-864b-12a4d739c029.history: Establishment of the State Bank of Morocco came about through an Act signed on 7 April 1906 at the Algeciras Conference by delegates from 12 European countries, the United States and Morocco. The bank was incorporated in February 1907 as a public limited company whose registered office was in Tangiers. Its capital was divided between the signatory countries, except the United States.
5381cedb-dcaf-5b98-864b-12a4d739c029.keywords: Economy; trade; banks; banking; financing; money; Europeans in Morocco; Andalusian architecture; Arab architecture; Islamic architecture; city; urban space; changes in urban space; European style banks; European economy; European financing
5381cedb-dcaf-5b98-864b-12a4d739c029.description2: After the State Bank of Tangier was built, the Moroccan state set up a network of banks and subsequently moved the headquarters of the Central Bank to Rabat. The buildings for this banking network were built in a similar Arab-Andalusian style, in most cases in sandstone.

5426a620-cbfc-5b20-bed9-14fa1801de7d.name: *Medjmouaï teçavir* (Collection de costumes)
5426a620-cbfc-5b20-bed9-14fa1801de7d.keywords: costume; diplomacy; fashion; court life; economy; finance; Ottoman; Tercüman; travel; traveller; Orientalism
5426a620-cbfc-5b20-bed9-14fa1801de7d.description2: Popular postcard from Turkey showing the costume worn by various people, according to occupation, activity, etc. At this time Turkish financial officials worked under European management.

54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.name: Dress
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.author: Huda Kilani
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.materials: Silk, cotton; hand woven Syrian silk fabric (brocade)
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.description2: This dress of al-Druze (Druse) women is made of a long grey with green and silver brocade, pursed narrow sleeves, wide, open square shaped chest, pursed at the middle and wide at the bottom with ruffles and a cotton liner. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation. The traditional Druse and other Jordanian costumes were influenced by the local trade and economic activities: as illustrated in this case, they were often made of silk textiles, produced in Syria and traded to Jordan and Palestine.

544117f8-c7fb-5075-b36e-315986c47bec.name: Transport plan of Beirut
544117f8-c7fb-5075-b36e-315986c47bec.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
544117f8-c7fb-5075-b36e-315986c47bec.description2: This map shows a plan of transport terminals in Beirut in 1891.

5483dab5-d84f-5427-be2a-f5641e4aecc1.name: Monthly revenues deriving from the traffic of boats through the Suez Canal sent by the consul of the Austro-Hungarian Empire in Port Said (Egypt) to the Commodities Exchange of Trieste
5483dab5-d84f-5427-be2a-f5641e4aecc1.author: Chiara Artico
5483dab5-d84f-5427-be2a-f5641e4aecc1.archival: ASTS, Deputazione di Borsa poi Camera di commercio di Trieste, b. 92, fasc. 1222.
5483dab5-d84f-5427-be2a-f5641e4aecc1.third_name: *Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez, Mouvement recettes, Septembre 1876.*
5483dab5-d84f-5427-be2a-f5641e4aecc1.description2: Out of the 109 boats that had passed through the Canal in that month, 78 were from Britain, 8 from France, 7 from the Netherlands and the remaining 16 were from Spain, Germany, Italy, Austria, Denmark and Norway. British ships passed through the Suez Canal on their way to India and to other British colonial possessions.

55244670-bd54-51f4-982e-13682dbb1443.name: A map of Tunisia (1:1,600,000) showing Italian agricultural settlements, mines, coral- and sponge-fishing areas and boat lines
55244670-bd54-51f4-982e-13682dbb1443.author: Giulia Barrera
55244670-bd54-51f4-982e-13682dbb1443.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906
55244670-bd54-51f4-982e-13682dbb1443.third_name: Carta della Tunisia protettorato francese, 1906 disegnata dal prof Cesidio Bonanni
55244670-bd54-51f4-982e-13682dbb1443.description2: The green rectangles on the map indicate Italian agricultural settlements; the number of settlers is indicated as well. In 1906 the majority of the Italian peasants had settled around Tunis and the Gulf of Hammamet. By contrast, few Italian peasants had settled in the South and in the interior of the country (the map indicated only 300 Italian peasants near Sfax and 400 near Kef).

56f05326-4b1d-5eff-9a58-a822374155ee.name: Portrait Of Binjamin Uziyel
56f05326-4b1d-5eff-9a58-a822374155ee.holder: The Quincentennial Foundation Museum, Archive of Turkish Jews
56f05326-4b1d-5eff-9a58-a822374155ee.keywords: Jewish community in Istanbul in 19th century; trade; sugar; commodities; markets
56f05326-4b1d-5eff-9a58-a822374155ee.description2: In 1911, when the Ottomans had to leave Tripoli, Binjamin Uziyel, who served in the consulate there, did research on a project of setting up sugar factories in Turkey after going to Genoa. He presented it to the Istanbul Chamber of Commerce by preparing a detailed report about setting up sugar factories in Turkey and ways to use the sugar beet.

5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.name: Wedding dress
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.author: Huda Kilani
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.materials: Linen and silk; hand woven and hand embroidered
5714f381-6e11-56d5-9801-fef85803c128.description2: Long black dress, wide at the bottom with narrow sleeves, rounded neck and open chest. Silk linen appliqué, hand embroidery with cross-stitch on the sides, back panel, chest, and sleeves with embroidered folkloric patterns. On the chest: necklace, cypress tree. Side: ivy, amulets, “feathers”. Front: small cypress tree on silk. Back: ivy, cypress tree, pillows, pasha tents. Sleeve: ivy, feather, triangle (amulets). Palestinian women's costumes varied according to each Palestinian city and geographical area. Costumes in the mountain regions were different from those of coastal and desert areas, and had a distinguished embroidery. This costume represents village style. Girls started preparing their trousseau (clothes, shawls and other belongings they collected for their marriage) at the age of ten. Married women's costumes were heavily embroidered. Palestinian weavers used traditional spinning processes using manual spindles to prepare the cotton and linen threads imported from Egypt. Ashkelon city weavers used light vertical hand looms (*Majdalawi* looms) to produce linen fabrics, while silk fabrics were spindled and woven in Syria.

57ffa9ee-eaef-5f59-b4a3-2237ac46b63a.name: The ivory trade
57ffa9ee-eaef-5f59-b4a3-2237ac46b63a.second_name: Transporting elephant tusks from Congo. Exhibition of the goods before sale in Anvers.
57ffa9ee-eaef-5f59-b4a3-2237ac46b63a.description2: Although banned in 1989, in the 19th century the ivory trade was flourishing. Many different objects, all marketed to a wealthy buyer, were made from this material: decorations, piano keys, knife handles, combs, fans, umbrella handles, and more.

585f44a9-1964-5231-b9ed-0ff3c0f07d5c.name: 5 Piastres
585f44a9-1964-5231-b9ed-0ff3c0f07d5c.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
585f44a9-1964-5231-b9ed-0ff3c0f07d5c.keywords: Commerce; trade; Currency; Coins; coinage; Numismatics
585f44a9-1964-5231-b9ed-0ff3c0f07d5c.description2: This 5 piastres bank note was printed by Bradbury Wilkinson and Co (BWC) without a watermark.

587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.name: Model of traditional pearling boat
587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.dates: Hegira first half of the 14th century / AD 20th century
587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.dimensions: Length 2334 mm, width 535 mm, height 395 mm
587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.description2: This type of boat represents the most common type of vessel that was involved in the pearling trade in Sharjah. Throughout the Arabian Gulf, several types of boats such as the Jalboot, Sambooq, Battil and the Sama'a, although in fact multi-purpose, were used for pearling at the peak of the industry in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Depending on the boat and size, the boats had the capacity to carry between 10 and 100 crew. This model is of the 'Saku', a Sama'a-type boat originally belonging to Juma Al Sari, the father of the model donor.

58b9f9f7-6b17-532d-8f51-0f4b19d4fb8d.name: *Vue d'Alger*
58b9f9f7-6b17-532d-8f51-0f4b19d4fb8d.author: Dalila Orfali
58b9f9f7-6b17-532d-8f51-0f4b19d4fb8d.description2: These two original lithographs depict the city of al-Jaza'ir (Algiers) prior to the English bombardment led by Lord Exmouth on 26 August 1816. The regency was ruled first by the *Beylerbeys* (general governors) from 1518 to 1587, then by the Pashas from 1587 to 1659, the *Aghas* from 1659 to 1671 and the Deys from 1671 to 1830. The reign of the final Dey of Algiers, Hussein, lasted 12 years until the French conquest in 1830.

59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.name: Belt
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.author: Huda Kilani
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.keywords: Leather; belt; embellished; niello; rosette buckles; silver
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.description2: Leather belt embellished with silver pieces decorated in niello with patterns and symbols at the end. Two silver rosette buckles at the end form a locking mechanism. This is an object produced by Circassian craftsmen. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries, with which they had spiritual and religious links. They brought with them their traditional activities, crafts and decorative patterns. All these elements soon mingled with the local Arab society and became part of the social and economic landscape of the Arab countries.

5a0832a0-d80b-5889-9b46-4a7e7fdf77f8.name: Pearl Trader’s Gauges
5a0832a0-d80b-5889-9b46-4a7e7fdf77f8.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
5a0832a0-d80b-5889-9b46-4a7e7fdf77f8.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
5a0832a0-d80b-5889-9b46-4a7e7fdf77f8.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
5a0832a0-d80b-5889-9b46-4a7e7fdf77f8.description2: These seven rectangular and foldable copper alloy gauges were used to ascertain the various sizes and circumferences of pearls, from the most miniscule to the gigantic, which would have fetched the highest price. When not in use, the implement was folded away and stored in a simple copper alloy sheath.

5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.name: Reliquary of St-George Chiopolites from Aivali
5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.author: Ballian 1992, 84, no. 44
5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.description2: The reliquary contained the head of George Chiopolites, who was martyred in Aïvali / Kydonies in 1807. The container made for the head has intricate rococo decoration with ribbons, bows, roses, blank heraldic shields and St George holding the attributes of a neomartyr under the imposing two-headed eagle of ecclesiastical authority. From the mid-eighteenth century, thanks to special administrative treatment or privileges, the inhabitants of Aïvali transformed what had been a small fishing village into a flourishing commercial centre on the Aeolian coast. The inscription on the reliquary refers to the goldsmith and to the Guild of Soap-Makers, which was one of the biggest trade associations in the town. It also refers to Sophronios, who oversaw the commissioning, and has been identified to the parish priest and a close relative of Theophilos Kaïris, a teacher at the Academy of Kydonies who was later expelled from the Church under the free Greek state for his revolutionary ideas and was to die in prison, the last ideologue of the Enlightenment.

en: Ballian, Anna, *Treasures from the Greek Communities of Asia Minor and Eastern Thrace. Collections from the Benaki Museum*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1992.

5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.name: Map of caravan routes
5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.author: Maria Francesca Carvelli (MWNF)
5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.archival: *The Geography of Africa*, London, Gill & Sons (publisher), 1897, p. 200
5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.keywords: Route; trade; pilgrimage; pilgrims; Muslim pilgrimage; Islam; Africa; religion; economy; Holy Places; Holy Cities; Hijaz; Makka; al-Madina; Jidda; Arab Peninsula
5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.description2: This map illustrates the trading caravan routes crossing the Sahara desert from Mediterranean ports (Tripoli, Tafilet, Tunis, Algiers and Oran) to sub-Saharan cities. The trading routes were connected north and south to three pilgrim routes for Mecca. The northern pilgrim route from Tunis and Tripoli included Siwah, Cairo, Suez and Aqaba. From Aqaba, meeting the pilgrim route from Damascus, it continued along the coast of Arabia to Mecca. The central route continued from Siwah through the oases of Dakkel and El-Kharjeh to ports on the Red Sea to Jeddah and Mecca. The southern route followed the valley of the Upper Niger through Timbuctu, Gao, Sokoto, Kano, Lake Chad and Kordofan to the port of Swakin on the Red Sea and continued to Jeddah by ship.

5d280899-351f-5ef7-95bb-ed98a12d141d.name: An open letter from the Tuscan community in Constantinople to the Chargé d’Affairs of Tuscany, protesting the detention of three Italian democrats exiled by Ottoman authorities
5d280899-351f-5ef7-95bb-ed98a12d141d.author: Massimo Sanacore
5d280899-351f-5ef7-95bb-ed98a12d141d.description2: Italian communities abroad actively supported the movement for Italian national unification known as “Risorgimento”. The Italian community in Constantinople raised funding to donate a cannon to the Kingdom of Sardinia, which in 1848 was at war with the Austrian Empire. After the Kingdom of Sardinia’s army was defeated, conflicts between the most moderate wing of the nationalist movement and the republicans (supporters of Giuseppe Mazzini) broke out and the Kingdom of Sardinia’s authorities started to persecute the latter.

5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.name: Brass head of flagpole
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.author: Huda Kilani
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.keywords: crescent shape; casted brass; wooden staff
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.description2: A crescent shape made of casted brass fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

5e2b03cb-5bee-5604-be76-35ecf0de0e45.name: *Valahian Caravan*
5e2b03cb-5bee-5604-be76-35ecf0de0e45.description2: In Wallachia and Moldavia transportation of merchandise by land was done similarly to the Arab and Ottoman world, but using big carts pulled by horses instead of camel caravans. Both the vehicle and a group of carts travelling together for commercial purposes were called "chervan”, a term derived from the Turkish word "kervan", meaning "caravan". The lithograph, depicting a carriage drawn by 12 horses and followed by a second vehicle, was printed in Vienna and its legend (*Wallachian carriage*) is written below the image in German, Hungarian and French.

5e9e845e-5f4e-508c-91ed-f52d967dbf97.name: *Family gathering in Alexandria*
5e9e845e-5f4e-508c-91ed-f52d967dbf97.author: Maria Dimitriadou
5e9e845e-5f4e-508c-91ed-f52d967dbf97.description2: Black and white photo in a family album: A family gathering at the garden of Emmanuel Benaki’s mansion in Alexandria. His eldest daughter Alexandra Benaki was engaged to his partner Tom Davis in April 1889. In the center of the picture appear the bride and the groom, the sister of Alexandra Benaki, Penelope Benaki-Delta, as well as their mother, Virginia Benaki. Phototographer unknown.

5ec581f1-3f8e-5a5c-bdc5-c2d1b4b525e3.name: A postcard advertising the Singer sewing machine and at the same time supporting Italian colonial expansion in Libya
5ec581f1-3f8e-5a5c-bdc5-c2d1b4b525e3.author: Giulia Barrera
5ec581f1-3f8e-5a5c-bdc5-c2d1b4b525e3.description2: This postcard sends the message that the Italian colonisers brought modernity to Libya. Both the sewing machine and the plane in the background epitomise modernity. The soldier is sewing an Italian flag. The postcard’s message is at the same time political and commercial.

5f941ae8-9023-5935-99ef-eaae452485b9.holder: The House of Antique Tin Boxes

601e5d3a-e68f-587a-846c-d0f3657cf4f6.name: *Dar al-Baladiyya, Damascus*
601e5d3a-e68f-587a-846c-d0f3657cf4f6.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
601e5d3a-e68f-587a-846c-d0f3657cf4f6.author: Stefan Weber
601e5d3a-e68f-587a-846c-d0f3657cf4f6.second_name: City Hall at the new urban centre at Merje Square
601e5d3a-e68f-587a-846c-d0f3657cf4f6.description2: Built between 1892 to 1894, the Dar al-Baladiyya was a prestigious edifice in stone. With its neo-classical elements and prominent middle projection, it was designed to display the power of the “new” state. The purpose of building the City Hall was functional, since the administrative workload, which rapidly increased after the reforms of the administrative system had to be accommodated.

61eb1293-6209-599c-bd83-34f180e3bec2.name: *The Port of Constanţa*
61eb1293-6209-599c-bd83-34f180e3bec2.description2: The Black Sea port of Constanța underwent its first modernization while Dobruja, the province where it is situated, was under Ottoman control. In 1857, when the Ottoman government hired a British company to build a railway in Dobruja, the concluded contract also stipulated the reconstruction of the Constanța port. Completed in 1864, it was still a small harbor with a wooden dock, a dam and one cereals depot. After Dobruja was annexed by Romania, a law was issued in 1885 for the “improvement and augmentation” of the port. In 1896 its modernization was leased to a French enterprise but due to some disagreements, three years later the state took over the works, which were led by architect Anghel Saligny. Inaugurated in 1909, the new port had 3 dams, several docks, depots, silos, an oil basin, an electric plant.

634af5db-b68c-5f95-9cf9-42e43802e5f2.name: A shop in Istanbul
634af5db-b68c-5f95-9cf9-42e43802e5f2.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)

634af5db-b68c-5f95-9cf9-42e43802e5f2.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century.

640180dd-059b-54fe-a33c-0700c3dd70f8.name: Photograph of the Beirut–Aleppo railway
640180dd-059b-54fe-a33c-0700c3dd70f8.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
640180dd-059b-54fe-a33c-0700c3dd70f8.keywords: Transport; Railway; Communication; Connection; Innovation; Aleppo; Lebanon
640180dd-059b-54fe-a33c-0700c3dd70f8.description2: The second railway built in Lebanon opened in 1906 and ran from Beirut to Aleppo in present-day Syria. It connected with the first railway line at Riyaq. The connection between Aleppo and Beirut, a well-equipped and sizeable port, decreased trade in Alexandretta, the traditional port for merchandise leaving or entering Syria. Alexandretta was not connected to Aleppo by rail until 1914. Aleppo and Northern Syria became increasingly important as links between Damascus and Beirut were consolidated. This also marked the increasing importance of Beirut as a powerful city in the region and not only as a Mediterranean port.

6466b53e-7366-59fb-b2d6-6c90c4bac6cd.name: Italian translation of the decree by the French Civil Affairs Superintendent (intendant civil) of Algeria, Louis-André Pichon, regulating coral fishing along the coasts of Algeria
6466b53e-7366-59fb-b2d6-6c90c4bac6cd.author: Cristina Francioli
6466b53e-7366-59fb-b2d6-6c90c4bac6cd.description2: This decree imposed a heavy tax on foreign ships that fished corals near Algerian shores, while exempting French ships. The decree was translated into Italian in Livorno, an active coral fishing port town that was badly affected by this ruling. Coral fishing was an important economic activity in the Mediterranean. Algeria was the main fishing area for corals, especially after the depletion of Sardinian coral.

64c7bc97-7cc3-58be-9d17-18bd4395053c.name: Map of Beirut's water networks

653ec3ae-d9cd-5520-a956-95f7ae1a6d21.keywords: Arabian Pensinsula; Emperor Franz I; coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; Hijaz; mint
653ec3ae-d9cd-5520-a956-95f7ae1a6d21.description2: This thaler was a large silver coin minted during the reign of Emperor Franz I (1804-1835). It was countersigned in the Arabic Peninsula at the mint of Hijaz around 1920.

66091ad7-e911-585b-ab5f-8072d134485c.name: The House of the Naboodah (Bayt al-Naboodah)
66091ad7-e911-585b-ab5f-8072d134485c.holder: Sharjah Museums Authority / Sharjah Heritage Directorate
66091ad7-e911-585b-ab5f-8072d134485c.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
66091ad7-e911-585b-ab5f-8072d134485c.notice: Please note that this is an unedited database entry and that it may contain grammatical errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are working to raise the funds required to complete the editing of the database; should you wish to contribute please visit our [Support page](https://www.museumwnf.org/atrium_support.php).
66091ad7-e911-585b-ab5f-8072d134485c.description2: This house at the heart of historic Sharjah belonged to 'Obaid bin 'Isa bin 'Ali Al Shamsi, who was also known as al-Naboodah. He was a well known pearl merchant with good connections to foreign countries such as India, East Africa and France. The house was originally built by 'Obaid's father Essa in 1845, and 'Obaid resided here with his three wives and ten children. Later it passed to his grandchildren, who lived in it till the 1970s. The double-storey house covers an area of 1280 square meters and is built around a large courtyard. Unusually, the kitchen annex with its well and the main reception area (*majlis*) are conceived separately from the main building arrangement. Family rooms and toilets are found on both floors, the first floor rooms preferably used in the summer, as they were cooler and airier than those on the ground floor. Enclosed rooms have high ceilings for the heat to rise and escape. Decoratively carved gypsum screen separate the rooms from washing areas. The house was carefully restored in the 1990s and now gives an excellent impression of the multiculturalism of traditional Sharjah architecture, as it combines local materials such as coral and lime mortar (*jus*) with red silt clay (*sarooj*) from Iran and hard woods from Zanzibar and East Africa.

673df29d-47f7-5309-b718-3f6340779d57.name: Tramway’s railway in Bliss Street
673df29d-47f7-5309-b718-3f6340779d57.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
673df29d-47f7-5309-b718-3f6340779d57.keywords: Transportation; road; commerce; urban development; Lebanon; Ottoman; Syria
673df29d-47f7-5309-b718-3f6340779d57.description2: The Beirut tramway was built in 1891 and ran through the centre of Beirut through to the coast, where it linked Beirut to Ma'ameltein.

67fb9e13-a6ba-5f67-8cea-07a7abdb3da1.name: Moroccan coins
67fb9e13-a6ba-5f67-8cea-07a7abdb3da1.description: Coin struck in 1903 under Mulay Sultan ‘Abd al-‘Aziz al-Hasan I (r. 1894 to 1908) at the mint in Fez. For a century (1800-1900) the ‘Alawid sultans struck coins in the workshops of Fez, but due to the economic crisis at the time, gold was unavailable so most coins were of silver, bronze or other common metals – although the technique remained the same, with the metal poured into moulds. The patterns on the face and on the back vary between the star with eight points (Solomon ring) and the indication of the place of mint.

685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.name: Wooden Sideboard with Mother of Pearl Inlay
685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Department
685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.dimensions: Height 2485 mm, width 1100 mm, depth 415 mm
685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
685a2ad1-af1f-51a1-a4f2-d4dc7fc2a7f0.description2: This tall, intricately carved sideboard consists of two parts, the mirror section with intricately carved openwork and mashrabiya ornamentation enhanced with mother-of-pearl inlay, and the narrow table section decorated with similar elements and with its four front legs supporting an elaborate system of lobed arches. the sideboard is further enhanced by religious inscriptions, some of which seem to suggest a Christian context. Sideboards and other European-style furniture were unknown in the Middle East until the second half of the12th/ 18th century. By the 13th/ 19th century, the urban elites in Ottoman cities enthusiastically imported domestic furniture from Italy, France and England or bought locally-made hybrid pieces that combined European and traditional Islamic elements like the item shown here. Many European entrepreneurs like the Italian Furino Brothers, based in Cairo, set up shop in Ottoman cities and specialised in this so-called Arabesque style, especially fashionable for furniture.

696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.name: Pin, plaque
696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.author: Huda Kilani
696bbefe-4763-59bf-ad00-3b86378355df.description2: A gold pin with three gold ¼ rashadi Ottoman coins welded together; at the end of two chains hang ¼ gold rashadi coins (Sultan Rashadi, 1909), each with a heart shape dangling from it. Ottoman coins were used as decorative objects for jewellery. Gold jewellery was usually bought only by the rich, while most people used silver jewellery. Pieces of gold or silver jewellery were given by the groom to the bride as a dowry, thus the choice of a piece of jewellery indicated the financial status of the groom.

69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.name: Marius Scalesi
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.holder: Institut Culturel Italien (Italian Emabassy in Tunisia)
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.keywords: Marius Scalesi; literature in French; poetry; migration
69f1c95c-2875-58ff-b85b-10d1c2d2ab83.description2: Pictured here is Marius (Mario) Scalesi, a young poet of Italian origin, born on 6 February 1892 in Tunis to an Italian father and a Maltese mother. He suffered from tuberculosis from birth, and became paralysed following a fall down the stairs in his home in La Goulette, the so-called "Little Sicily" of Tunis. Forced to abandon his studies in order to make a living, he completed his education independently. His articles of literary criticism and poems were published in the journal *La Tunisie Illustrée*. His collection of poems, *Les Poèmes d'un Maudit* sheds light on the hardships of his life. He died in 1922 in an asylum in Palermo. A fascinating figure due to his triple cultural identity - Italian, French and Tunisian - he is considered one of the pioneers of North African poetry in French.

6a34e64b-e996-5c58-9984-ac149359cb8c.name: 100 Piastres
6a34e64b-e996-5c58-9984-ac149359cb8c.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
