6a34e64b-e996-5c58-9984-ac149359cb8c.description2: This 100 piastres bank note bears no watermark, and is illustrated with horses, symbolising pride, and the famous columns of the Baalbek temple.

6acad3a4-63f3-5160-bf8e-60081e141ee0.name: Street map of Beirut
6acad3a4-63f3-5160-bf8e-60081e141ee0.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
6acad3a4-63f3-5160-bf8e-60081e141ee0.keywords: Commerce; Map; Streets; Shops; Railway; Maritime
6acad3a4-63f3-5160-bf8e-60081e141ee0.description2: This map of Beirut was drawn in in 1902 under the reign of Sultan 'Abd al-Hamid II. The table on the left contains a numbered list of shops and important landmarks, whereas the table on the right lists the name and location of Beirut's railway and maritime companies.

6b87d037-edfd-580b-a728-429fe7822c7b.name: Map of Beirut
6b87d037-edfd-580b-a728-429fe7822c7b.holder: American University of Beirut, Jafet Library, Archives and Special Collections Department
6b87d037-edfd-580b-a728-429fe7822c7b.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
6b87d037-edfd-580b-a728-429fe7822c7b.keywords: Expansion; Map; Districts; Consulates; Routes; City; Beirut
6b87d037-edfd-580b-a728-429fe7822c7b.description2: This map dates to 1876 and was drawn by the acting Danish Consul, Julius Loytved for the Sultan 'Abd al-Hamid II. Loytved was a map-maker, an archaeologist, and the director of various Anglo-Syrian schools. This detailed survey map includes 12 districts of Beirut: 1 - The Old City and the *suq*; 2 - Al-Zaytuna; 3 - Ras Beirut; 4 - Msaytbe; 5 - Mazraat al-Arab; 6 - Ras el-Naba'; 7 - Al-Bashura; 8 - Achrafieh; 9 - St. Dimitri; 10 - Mimas; 11 - Rmeil; 12 - Al-Saifi. The roads to Damascus, Saida and Tripoli are all clearly indicated by emphasis on the edge of the map. The map also indicates 47 other points of interest, including 91 consulates, military posts, government buildings, educational and health institutions, public parks, private gardens, cemeteries, archaeological sites, and sand and rock hills.

6dac0c9a-9cc8-5832-9efa-512fe3c88e4f.name: The Palace of Porto Trade Association Headquarters, the Arabian Room
6dac0c9a-9cc8-5832-9efa-512fe3c88e4f.history: During the siege of Porto (1832-33) by Miguelist Army led by absolutist Prince Miguel (1802-66) against the Liberal troops of his brother Prince Pedro (1798-1834), S. Francisco convent was burnt only surviving the church.  Porto Trade Association’s headquarters was erected over these ruins. Queen Maria II issued the law concession letter of 19th June 1841 to order the establishment of the Stock Exchange and the Trial Court. The solemn placing of the first stone took place on 6 October 1842.
6dac0c9a-9cc8-5832-9efa-512fe3c88e4f.keywords: Oporto; Trade Association; cultural heritage; trade; Queen Maria II; Cabralism
6dac0c9a-9cc8-5832-9efa-512fe3c88e4f.architects: Architects: Joaquim da Costa Lima (1840–1860), Gustavo Adolpho Gonçalves e Sousa (1860–1879), Thomaz Augusto Soller (1879–1883), José de Macedo Araújo Júnior (1883–1890), Joel da Silva Pereira (1894–1899) and José Marques da Silva (1889–1910); Painting and sculptures: Luigi Maninin, António Ramalho, António Carneiro, Veloso Salgado, Marques de Oliveira, Soares dos Reis, Eduardo Malta, Teixeira Lopes and Henrique Medina, among others.
6dac0c9a-9cc8-5832-9efa-512fe3c88e4f.description2: The Arabian Room (1862–1880) is considered as the most emblematic of all the Palace’s rooms, embodying the Neo-Moorish art in Portugal. Inspired by the Palace of Alhambra in Granada combines the Arab ornament grammar and the fertile imagination of the engineer/architect, Gustavo Adolpho Gonçalves e Sousa. The Hall of Nations is decorated with the national shield and the coat of arms of the countries with which Portugal had the closest ties of friendship and trade; consolidating the idea that the greatness of a nation, country or region is not a singular effort, but one of union, strength and the cooperation among people of different nations.

6e335928-9fa2-5b6f-93cb-9088b371f464.name: *Zabun*
6e335928-9fa2-5b6f-93cb-9088b371f464.description2: The *zabun* is similar to a European coat and the Turkish *qaftan* (a European inspired coat). It is speculated that it first arrived in the eastern part of Saudi Arabia through the Hajj, at the time of the Turkish empire, and later became popular in Qatar and Bahrayn. The *zabun* is made out of fine Indian Kashmiri brown wool with intricate embroidery. Decoration: made of light brown wool embroidered with *boteh* design, motif across the coat – paisley, Islamic decorative arts. Imitated because the shape is Kashmiri, shaped like cashew nut, pronounced ‘Gazorah.’ Colours are red, yellow, and edges are lined with metal silk thread – round neck opening. Narrow Nehru collar, or Chinese collar is known in Qatar. Buttons are handmade metal balls down the front. It is worn with the *thawb ishlahat*.

6f1032fa-b287-57a0-81ee-3a8c6977d38a.name: The Palace of Porto Trade Association Headquarters
6f1032fa-b287-57a0-81ee-3a8c6977d38a.history: During the siege of Porto (1832-33) by Miguelist Army led by absolutist Prince Miguel (1802-66) against the Liberal troops of his brother Prince Pedro (1798-1834), S. Francisco convent was burnt only surviving the church.  Porto Trade Association’s headquarters was erected over these ruins. Queen Maria II issued the law concession letter of 19th June 1841 to order the establishment of the Stock Exchange and the Trial Court. The solemn placing of the first stone took place on 6 October 1842.
6f1032fa-b287-57a0-81ee-3a8c6977d38a.architects: Architects: Joaquim da Costa Lima (1840–1860), Gustavo Adolpho Gonçalves e Sousa (1860–1879), Thomaz Augusto Soller (1879–1883), José de Macedo Araújo Júnior (1883–1890), Joel da Silva Pereira (1894–1899) and José Marques da Silva (1889–1910); Painting and sculptures: Luigi Maninin, António Ramalho, António Carneiro, Veloso Salgado, Marques de Oliveira, Soares dos Reis, Eduardo Malta, Teixeira Lopes and Henrique Medina, among others.
6f1032fa-b287-57a0-81ee-3a8c6977d38a.description2: All the rooms of the Palácio da Bolsa are works of art, with undisputed prominence as a worthy representative of the city of Porto. Along three generations, great names in architecture, painting, sculpture and decorative arts contributed to the creation of a unique heritage at the Palácio da Bolsa, a true jewel of the neo-classical style of the 19th century. In the Palace’s interior, along with the grand architectural design of the Hall of Nations and the famous Arab Room, other noteworthy attractions include: the furniture’s symbolic meaning and its aesthetic originality; the decorative stucco’s’ intricate detail; the masterful detail of the wooden inlaid floors; the coat of arms and heraldic representations; finely sculpted statues and an immense profusion of gigantic oil paintings and frescos by great Portuguese masters.

7080a158-a1b4-545b-bb83-ebdc891f29f8.name: Moroccan coins
7080a158-a1b4-545b-bb83-ebdc891f29f8.description: Coin struck in 1903 under Mulay Sultan ‘Abd al-‘Aziz al-Hasan I (r. 1894 to 1908) at the mint in Fez. For a century (1800-1900) the ‘Alawid sultans struck coins in the workshops of Fez, but due to the economic crisis at the time, gold was unavailable so most coins were of silver, bronze or other common metals – although the technique remained the same, with the metal poured into moulds. The patterns on the face and on the back vary between the star with eight points (Solomon ring) and the indication of the place of mint.
7080a158-a1b4-545b-bb83-ebdc891f29f8.keywords: Coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; gold; silver; bronze; mint; moulding; moulds; six-pointed star; ring; workshop; traditional coinage; European influence

70ae613d-6258-52dc-8ef3-3c83dcfa4fb0.name: *Turkish café, Smyrna, 9 November 1837*
70ae613d-6258-52dc-8ef3-3c83dcfa4fb0.second_name: Taken from *Voyage dans la Russie Méridionale et la Crimée* (Traveling in southern Russia and the Crimea)
70ae613d-6258-52dc-8ef3-3c83dcfa4fb0.description2: Denis-Auguste-Marie Raffet (1804–1860), sketcher and painter, travelled to Southern Russia, Crimea and Turkey with the Prince Demidoff in 1837. He brought back with him a few hundred illustrated pages, which were published in *Voyage en Crimée*. This image, depicting a café in Smyrna (Izmir), the "Little Paris" of the Ottoman Empire, is an excellent example of Orientalist drawing.

70c03f94-1563-5fc4-9b32-84ea00fd8d52.name: A Letter from the State Bank of Morocco
70c03f94-1563-5fc4-9b32-84ea00fd8d52.description: Correspondence between the State Bank and Moroccan central government from the archive of Muhammad al-Muqri, the Grand Vizier of Finance under Sultan Mulay ‘Abd al-Hafiz al-Hasan I.
70c03f94-1563-5fc4-9b32-84ea00fd8d52.keywords: Economy; finance; banking; French in Morocco; credit; protectorate

71bafc31-de50-5515-8301-3411a7a0be01.name: *A market in Bucharest*
71bafc31-de50-5515-8301-3411a7a0be01.description2: Wallachia and Moldavia's contacts with the Ottoman Empire also influenced the aspect of Romanian cities. For example, marketplaces, as known from 19th century paintings and lithographs, were similar to Turkish bazaars and represented, just like in the Ottoman Empire, the commercial centre of a city. The watercolor is part of an album with reproductions after 15 of Amedeo Preziosi’s paintings that depict scenes from Bucharest. Maltese painter Amedeo Preziosi met Carol of Hohenzollern, ruler of Romania, in Istanbul in 1866. Invited by the prince to come visit his country, Preziosi was in Romania between June-July 1868 and May-July 1869. He is the author of more than 250 works inspired by Romanian landscapes, cities and people.

73c32255-eecb-5121-b674-c388b401bbb6.name: Charcoal iron
73c32255-eecb-5121-b674-c388b401bbb6.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
73c32255-eecb-5121-b674-c388b401bbb6.author: Huda Kilani
73c32255-eecb-5121-b674-c388b401bbb6.description2: A heavy iron box with a triangle-shaped lid with a handle and a hollow interior that could hold smouldering charcoal to keep the iron hot. This object of everyday use illustrates how the changes in mundane life affected society at a global level. Objects like this were traded locally within Jordan.

73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.name: Headdress
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.author: Huda Kilani
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.keywords: silver; prominent dome; disk; al- Druz women
73e736ab-49ec-5eea-8f27-af65046fe133.description2: A silver circular disk with filigree work and prominent dome above; chains dangling with triple petal and filigree work at the end; placed on the top of a high hat worn by al-Druze (Druse) women. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and the demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

74dafe7a-b3e7-5be6-b35d-e97ef0242008.name: The cruiser Bascir during a test voyage at sea
74dafe7a-b3e7-5be6-b35d-e97ef0242008.author: Daniela Tazzi
74dafe7a-b3e7-5be6-b35d-e97ef0242008.archival: ASLi, Cantiere Navale Luigi Orlando, cassetta 33, lastra 91
74dafe7a-b3e7-5be6-b35d-e97ef0242008.description2:
In 1890, political pressure from Italian Prime Minister Francesco Crispi secured construction of the cruiser Bascir for the Moroccan Navy for the Fratelli Orlando shipyards located in Livorno (Italy), winning against French competitors.  
The Bascir was the first cruiser built by an Italian shipyard for a foreign navy after Italian unification in 1860. It was delivered to Morocco in 1894. Among its amenities was a hamam (in Western Europe often known as Turkish Bath), expressly requested by the buyer.  
The Fratelli Orlando shipyards also built a yacht for the Khédivé of Egypt.

74e93f42-b022-5056-9d51-bed2d2eb0ca5.name: *Map of Algeria's commercial routes to the "Pays des Noirs"* \[Guinea\]
74e93f42-b022-5056-9d51-bed2d2eb0ca5.description2: Having conquered Algeria, France launched several expeditions in order to open up new trade routes from North Africa to Guinea. Europeans had great difficulty in using the internal trade routes, which were controlled by indigenous African kingdoms, so were instead limited to coastal routes.

75891604-fdb8-540e-af25-a6509a9103f7.name: *Cairo: houses and gardens in the French quarter.* Flaubert in the foreground.
75891604-fdb8-540e-af25-a6509a9103f7.description2: The writer Gustave Flaubert lived in Egypt for three years from 1849 to 1851 with his friend Maxime Du Camp. He saw and experienced many new things during this time, travelling to Egypt, Beirut, Jerusalem and Damascus. Although Gustave Flaubert did not like being photographed, Maxime du Camp was able to take this snap of him in Cairo.

7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.name: Pearl Grading Sieves
7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.description2: These copper alloy sieves were used to grade pearls into their various sizes. The larger, heavier and more luminous a pearl was, the higher its price.These pearl sieves were known as tus or tasat (sing. Tasa). Carefully graded, they are deep circular vessels, their bases pierced and designed to fit one into the other. According to local sources, sets could consists of between four and 45 units. Traditionally, these pearl sieves were used by the tawwash or sea-going merchant, who carried them in a characteristic cloth bag or dasta, when he visited the pearlers, together with all the other implements of his trade, i.e. portable scales and agate weights, a pearl scoop, and his table for calculating the value of the pearls.

7c98ed41-590d-5c29-bafe-19140f7e1bc3.name: İzmir Port
7c98ed41-590d-5c29-bafe-19140f7e1bc3.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
7c98ed41-590d-5c29-bafe-19140f7e1bc3.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; İzmir; Port; trade
7c98ed41-590d-5c29-bafe-19140f7e1bc3.description2: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. İzmir Port, due to its geopolitical position, is the gateway to western Turkey. As a result of growth in world trade and increases of raw material needs due to the industrial revolution, İzmir Port was the most important trade route in the 19th century. Construction of new railways in the Ottoman period increased commercial activity.

7d6b2d8b-aee7-5a0e-bbaf-f3702ae0946a.name: A commercial artery of 19th-century Bucharest
7d6b2d8b-aee7-5a0e-bbaf-f3702ae0946a.description2: Mentioned in documents since the 16th century, this street, one of the oldest in Bucharest, connected the centre of the city with an area situated east of it, where a trade fair took place annually. Because of this, the street was called “The Bridge of the Outside Fair” (in the past the major streets of Bucharest used to be called “bridges” because they used to be covered with wooden boards). In time, as the fair was gradually moved eastwards, the street was extended. On both its sides there used to be many shops, inns, restaurants, craftsmen’s workshops.

825ea881-372b-5499-bcbe-096246ecd917.name: Import/export activities between Egypt and Venice in 1868 and the first six months of 1869
825ea881-372b-5499-bcbe-096246ecd917.author: Andrea Pelizza
825ea881-372b-5499-bcbe-096246ecd917.archival:
*Memoria della Commissione nominata dalla Camera di Commercio ed arti di Venezia ed incaricata di dimostrare l’utilità derivante alla nazione dal progetto di legge presentato alla Camera dei deputati dal sig. ministro del lavori pubblici nella tornata dell’8 marzo 1869, e concernente la nuova convenzione colla Società anonima italiana di navigazione Adriatico-Orientale pel prolungamento sino a Venezia del servizio postale e commerciale marittimo tra l’Italia e l’Egitto*.  
Supplement to the *Giornale ufficiale della Camera di commercio ed arti di Venezia*, 21 March 1869, no. 12.  
ASVe, Camera di Commercio di Venezia, I serie, b. 422, anno 1869
825ea881-372b-5499-bcbe-096246ecd917.description2: The items imported from Egypt were cotton, natron (a hydrous native sodium carbonate, used in chemical industry; Egypt had a rich deposit of it in Wadi el-Natrun), coffee, hides, fruit, copper and tamarind roots. The items exported to Egypt included wood and pieces of furniture, fruits and vegetables, butter, bricks and tiles, glass beads, lime, wine, cloth, medicaments, books, and various other products.

83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.name: Lace skirt
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.author: Huda Kilani
83550dcd-d5fe-53bf-ba81-33534dbf86ed.description2: Skirt of light pink lace with black flowers, pursed from the middle, worn over a woman’s dress. This object illustrates the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the various local costumes and rites, fashion and personal attire. This skirt was used by al-Druze women in Jordan. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

837581e0-006f-52d2-82bf-795b4cf10463.name: Portrait of Abraham Behor And Nisim Camondo
837581e0-006f-52d2-82bf-795b4cf10463.holder: The Quincentennial Foundation Museum, Zulfaris Synagogue Museum
837581e0-006f-52d2-82bf-795b4cf10463.description2: Abraham Salomon's descendants, Abraham-Behor (1829-1889) and Nisim (1830-1889) were partners in banking. As a rival to the Ottoman Bank, The Camondo Family established the Ottoman Empire Company-i Umumiyesi (*Societe Generale de l'Empire Ottoman*) with a capital of two million pounds in 1864. Because of the establishment of the Credit General Ottoman Bank in 1868, the Camondo Brothers decided to move the bank to Paris with the idea that the Bank should have absolutely no external links. Abraham-Behor became president of the institution of the *Alliance Israelite Universelle* in 1864. This institution – which instructed students in French in the name of modernization and westernization – was founded to improve the material and spiritual conditions of the Jews and to ensure the spread of education in İstanbul.

83c3fe83-79b0-588d-a540-cb63c72ac1b4.name: Pearling Scales Case
83c3fe83-79b0-588d-a540-cb63c72ac1b4.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
83c3fe83-79b0-588d-a540-cb63c72ac1b4.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
83c3fe83-79b0-588d-a540-cb63c72ac1b4.description2: Pearling scales were an essential tool for any pearl merchant. All aspects of a pearl’s physical appearance – its shape, hue, perfection, size and indeed weight all determined its value and saleability. This copper alloy case for pearling scales is of the characteristic type common in the pearling industry throughout the Gulf. It combines a very slightly pointed, circular section designed to receive the two small bowls of the scales, with a narrow elongated section to contain the balance, with the scales's strings carefully wound around it for storage. This example is particularly interesting in that it appears to give the name of the merchant and the date 1280 H/ 1863 AD.

841ba735-7c60-5603-8827-b02f6aedad8e.name: Arab coffee pot
841ba735-7c60-5603-8827-b02f6aedad8e.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
841ba735-7c60-5603-8827-b02f6aedad8e.author: Huda Kilani
841ba735-7c60-5603-8827-b02f6aedad8e.description2: One padded handle with leather, tapered cover; long covered nozzle, stamped reliefs. Coffee-drinking in a communal setting is an essential part of traditions in Bedouin communities to celebrate or mourn. This object of common use reflects the Bedouins’ traditions and everyday life and illustrates the variegated population composition of the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

842a5200-0594-5a9c-bea6-e441fe3c4f78.name: Faience pottery tile
842a5200-0594-5a9c-bea6-e441fe3c4f78.author: Houria Cherid
842a5200-0594-5a9c-bea6-e441fe3c4f78.description2: This faience pottery tile is painted with a ship in a circle in its centre, surrounded by flying birds. The rest of the *zelige* tile is decorated with a stylised floral pattern in each of its four corners.

8450e17b-8c6f-5b90-8443-1e6a14d55b9e.name: Orosdi-Back
8450e17b-8c6f-5b90-8443-1e6a14d55b9e.bibliography: Kupferschmidt, Uri, *The Orosdi-Back Saga: European Department Stores and Middle Eastern Consumers*, Istanbul: OBARC, 2007.
8450e17b-8c6f-5b90-8443-1e6a14d55b9e.author: Ahmad al-Bindari
8450e17b-8c6f-5b90-8443-1e6a14d55b9e.history: The Orosdi-Back story starts in Hungary with the liaison of two families when Adolf Orosdi’s sister, Antoinette (?-1879), married Maurice Back. Given that they were Jewish and had supported the Hungarian rebellion against the Austrian Empire, Adolf Orosdi and Maurice Back settled in Galata district in Istanbul, a focal point for Jews and one of the Ottoman Empire’s most vibrant business centres. In 1855, they established their shop under the name of Omar Effendi. The Orosdi-Back enterprise expanded from there, and their branches were given the combined name “Orosdi-Back”. It had outlets in Constantinople, Adana, Izmir, Samsun, Cairo, Alexandria, Port-Said, Zagazig, Tanta, Tunis, Philippopoli (Plovdiv), Bucharest, Aleppo, Beirut, Salonica, Tabriz, Tehran, Casablanca, Meknes, Vienna from 1893 and Basra and Baghdad after WWI.
8450e17b-8c6f-5b90-8443-1e6a14d55b9e.keywords: Orosdi-Back; Omar Effendi; Etablishements Orosdi-Back "Omar Effendi"; department store; architecture; Art Nouveau; Neo Baroque
8450e17b-8c6f-5b90-8443-1e6a14d55b9e.description2: Modern Egypt and cosmopolitan Cairo emerged in the context of diverse foreign communities and their interaction with Egyptians. By the turn of the 20th century, this cultural exchange gave birth to a new kind of commercial activity: big department stores (*grands magasins*), a novelty that developed more or less at the same time as it did in Europe. Foremost amongst these was Orosdi-Back, one of the largest department stores in Egypt, whose rivals included Cicurel, Chémla, Sednaoui and others. Raoul Brandon, a French Jewish architect, designed the Orosdi-Back premises in the corner of two important streets, \`Abd al-Aziz and Rushdi Pasha, in 1906. He designed a building with glamour *à la parisiènne*, evoking the elegant department stores of Paris, in Neo-Baroque style with a glimpse of Art Nouveau flair in its lines.

84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.name: *Entrance to Damascus*
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.artist: W. H. McFarlane (after a drawing by Harry Fenn 1838 – 1911)
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.description2: This coloured engraving by W. H. McFarlane shows the entrance to Damascus by the new French-built road through the Merj, or meadow, west of the city. Most probably this is the carriage road that had been established between Beirut and Damascus in 1863, at a time when most other connecting arterties were mere mule paths. French firms also built railways and ports in Syria during the later 19th century. The Ottoman style building in the background on the right is the Tekkiye Mosque Complex, built on the banks of the Barada river at the orders of Suleiman the Magnificent between 1554-1560 and incorporating a mosque, accomodation, a soup kitchen and a hospice.

863f2655-60dd-5322-acff-d958595ed2e2.name: *Società d'Esplorazione Commerciale in Africa*
863f2655-60dd-5322-acff-d958595ed2e2.second_name: Taken from *Carta economica della Tripolitana e Cirenaica, colle ultime esplorazioni, 1880-81-82 (ed. 1884)*
863f2655-60dd-5322-acff-d958595ed2e2.description2: This map shows Italian commercial expeditions in Africa, particularly in Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, between the years 1881 and 1882. In the search for a colonial empire Italy particularly targeted Libyan territory, for political and economic reasons, as well as for its proximity and the fact it once belonged to the Roman Empire.

868c8876-a63c-5812-a3d6-8c1fbf7d0e19.name: *Panoramic view of the Isthmus of the Suez, tracing the canal between the two seas*
868c8876-a63c-5812-a3d6-8c1fbf7d0e19.artist: Louis Maurice Adolphe Linant de Bellefonds
868c8876-a63c-5812-a3d6-8c1fbf7d0e19.keywords: Suez canal; Egypt; Ferdinand de Lesseps
868c8876-a63c-5812-a3d6-8c1fbf7d0e19.description2: Between 1859 and 1869, the Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez built a canal joining the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, thus opening up a strategic trade route towards the Indian subcontinent. This panoramic image was drawn by Louis Maurice Adolphe Linant de Bellefonds (1798–1883), artist and explorer fascinated with Egypt who played a key role, alongside Ferdinand de Lesseps, in the planning and construction of the Suez Canal.

869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.name: La Goulette
869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
869766dc-71ca-53a7-b67f-e1ed2b58d4ac.description2: The expansion of the city of Tunis necessitated the construction of a large modern port which would be accessible to large-tonnage ships. Thus, in the early years of the French protectorate, the port of Tunis, La Goulette, saw a sharp increase in traffic. As well as a fishing port, the primary function of La Goulette, it also became an industrial centre thanks to the construction of a power plant on the north side of the canal, which served the tramways and the electric railway going to the northern suburbs. Finally, on the eve of the war, La Goulette had also become a residential town, particularly popular in summer for its seaside resorts.

86f5889a-6b8e-56da-8202-c0ca7f73045b.name: Algerian Corkmaker [Paris Exhibition, 1878]
86f5889a-6b8e-56da-8202-c0ca7f73045b.author: Marina Minozzi
86f5889a-6b8e-56da-8202-c0ca7f73045b.archival: *L'Esposizione di Parigi del 1878 illustrata*, Sonzogno Editore, 1878, p. 212
86f5889a-6b8e-56da-8202-c0ca7f73045b.keywords: Exposition universelle de Paris; industrialisation; exhibition building; Moorish city; exhibitions and urban spaces; Moorish style; Islamic architecture; reinterpretation; exoticism; reproduction; model; magazine
86f5889a-6b8e-56da-8202-c0ca7f73045b.copyright: Copyright image: Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Roma.
86f5889a-6b8e-56da-8202-c0ca7f73045b.description2: At the International Exhibition in Paris, 1878, commercial activities typical of the colony were performed in the park next to Trocadero Pavilion, as part of the reconstruction of a hypothetical typical neighbourhood. The making of cork-taps was moved from Europe to Algeria to take advantage from the numerous Algerian forests. Taps were both made by hand and by machines and were brought to Europe from Trocadero.

879c6b5d-7835-5885-8c9b-1e2618fa25ae.name: Coin
879c6b5d-7835-5885-8c9b-1e2618fa25ae.holder: Musée de la Monnaie : Banque Centrale de Tunisie
879c6b5d-7835-5885-8c9b-1e2618fa25ae.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
879c6b5d-7835-5885-8c9b-1e2618fa25ae.description2: This coin dating from the reign of is inscribed on one side with "20 francs" written in Arabic, the year 1325 from the Hijri calendar, and framed by an olive branch on the right and a palm leaf on the left. The reverse is inscribed with "20 francs" written in French, "Tunisia" and the year 1907, framed by a beaded border which is then decorated with two flower-stem reliefs, a crescent at the bottom and a star at the top.

87e89e1f-16b1-5dc6-9a0f-3df85a103fa8.name: Moroccan coins
87e89e1f-16b1-5dc6-9a0f-3df85a103fa8.description: Coin struck in 1903 under Mulay Sultan ‘Abd al-‘Aziz al-Hasan I (r. 1894 to 1908) at the mint in Fez. For a century (1800-1900) the ‘Alawid sultans struck coins in the workshops of Fez, but due to the economic crisis at the time, gold was unavailable so most coins were of silver, bronze or other common metals – although the technique remained the same, with the metal poured into moulds. The patterns on the face and on the back vary between the star with eight points (Solomon ring) and the indication of the place of mint.
87e89e1f-16b1-5dc6-9a0f-3df85a103fa8.holder: Numismatic Museum of the al-Maghreb Bank
87e89e1f-16b1-5dc6-9a0f-3df85a103fa8.keywords: Coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; gold; silver; bronze; mint; moulding; moulds; six-pointed star; ring; workshop; traditional coinage; European influence

884d9ccd-97ec-51c8-aec6-d384ad59224c.name: A Tunisian decoration (on the right) and an Italian decoration (on the left) awarded to a member of the Moreno family
884d9ccd-97ec-51c8-aec6-d384ad59224c.author: Massimo Sanacore
884d9ccd-97ec-51c8-aec6-d384ad59224c.archival: ASLi, Famiglia Moreno di Tunisi, b. 17
884d9ccd-97ec-51c8-aec6-d384ad59224c.description2:
Two members of the Moreno family, Raffaello (Tunis 1844-1913) and his brother Leone (Tunis, 1852-1940) were awarded honours both by the Italian King (Cavaliere dell’Ordine della Corona d’Italia) and by the Bey of Tunis (Nichan Iftikhar). The Morenos were Jews from Livorno (Italy), who had migrated to Tunisia in the early 19th century.  
Other Italians migrants in Tunisia were awarded both the title of Cavaliere dell’Ordine della Corona d’Italia by the Italian King and the title of Nichan Iftikhar by the Bey of Tunis, including Giuseppe Di Vittorio (a Sicilian who ran a construction company) and Luigi Rey (born in Tunis to an immigrant family from a village north of Turin, Piedmont, Italy, who also ran a construction company) and the Jewish Doctor Giacomo Castelnuovo.

888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.name: Ring
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.author: Huda Kilani
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.keywords: Floral decoration; religious objects; waqf; Qur’an; Ottoman Baroque-Rococo
888046f7-3ef2-5941-9017-769431669b16.description2:
Thin silver ring with a squared black stone set in silver. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom.  
Jordan's economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for this purpose. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

894e770e-bdda-5d94-ae6c-90aaf47244ae.name: Beirut–Damascus Railway Company headquaters
894e770e-bdda-5d94-ae6c-90aaf47244ae.holder: Railway and Public Transportation Authority, Ministry of Transportation
894e770e-bdda-5d94-ae6c-90aaf47244ae.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Rita El Hachem
894e770e-bdda-5d94-ae6c-90aaf47244ae.description2: This photograph shows the headquarters of Lebanon Railway Company in Beirut.

8a58f4f9-1644-5ff0-8f2d-9e17a9b86098.name: Bills from the Beirut Tramway and Electricity company
8a58f4f9-1644-5ff0-8f2d-9e17a9b86098.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
8a58f4f9-1644-5ff0-8f2d-9e17a9b86098.description2: Two bills from the Beirut Tramway Company. The first is for the value of 22 Ottoman pounds, and is dated to 1 February 1896. The second is for the value of 11 Ottoman pounds and is dated to 1 November 1990.

8b6d48f1-d450-5891-bb54-198e8d16fb19.name: Geographical Society, Portugal’s Room
8b6d48f1-d450-5891-bb54-198e8d16fb19.holder: Photography Archive, Lisbon City Council, CML
8b6d48f1-d450-5891-bb54-198e8d16fb19.author: Ema Pires
8b6d48f1-d450-5891-bb54-198e8d16fb19.description2: General view of the interior of Portugal’s Room, at Lisbon’s Geographical Society. A set of seven flags decorates the galleries. There are three floors furnished with book shelves. In the ground floor, there are also a large number of chairs. A group of people is also visible here.

8ca42471-fa97-56f9-94ac-a3f4088b69ff.name: Cannon
8ca42471-fa97-56f9-94ac-a3f4088b69ff.holder: Palais de la Rose – Musée de l’Armée
8ca42471-fa97-56f9-94ac-a3f4088b69ff.author: Bechir Yazidi
8ca42471-fa97-56f9-94ac-a3f4088b69ff.keywords: Tunisian army; Musée de l'Armée; Palais de la Rose
8ca42471-fa97-56f9-94ac-a3f4088b69ff.description2: This cast bronze cannon is 156 cm long, has a front diameter of 50 cm and a back diameter of 85 cm. The Beylik of Tunis' coat of arms can be seen near the muzzle, and the Kingdom of Italy's near the back, as well as the name of the manufacturer, Fonderia di Torino, and the date, 1867.

8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.name: Headdress
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.author: Huda Kilani
8d188108-655f-550e-b130-a0eb24f32b9c.description2: Three bands of silver (800) chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head; 1/4 Ottoman coins (*barah*s) are fixed in the inner section of the band. This kind of jewellery was part of the dowry the groom gave to the bride. Dowries consisted mostly of silver jewellery because only the rich could afford gold jewellery. Thus, the financial status of the groom was highlighted by the jewellery he could give as a dowry and by the use of coins as pieces of jewellery for his wife.

8f457f6a-6cb0-596d-bc20-07d4baa579f5.name: *Commercial map, or chart, of the industries, communication lines and main nautical flags and ports of the states of Europe.*

8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.name: Beirut Port before expansion
8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury, Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.keywords: Commerce; Expansion; Economy; Trading; Goods; Transportation; Port; Harbor; Communication; Beirut
8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.description2: This photograph shows the Beirut port before its expansion. The dam was built under the command of Ibrahim Pasha. This old port underwent several important changes in the late 19th century, including the construction of a commercial tribunal and expansion of the port. This expansion involved the enlargement of existing buildings and filling areas of sea with rock brought in along the Nahr al-Kalb railway.

90753f8b-1041-579e-af7d-41a335a9669a.name: Black Sea: Sevastopol port
90753f8b-1041-579e-af7d-41a335a9669a.description2: Founded by Yekaterina II (Catherine the Great) in 1783, Sevastopol became a very active military and commercial port following the Russian annexation of the Crimea. The siege of Sevastopol from 1854 to 1855 was the one of the most critical points of the Crimean War.

90898679-94a2-5a74-9442-dce1eaec5acf.name: *Shepherd with his sheep*
90898679-94a2-5a74-9442-dce1eaec5acf.description2: Sheep husbandry has always been a traditional agricultural occupation in the Romanian lands. Shepherds spent summers in mountainous regions, where they found pastures for their flocks, and descended into lower valleys for the winter. Transhumance is still practiced in Romania. During the Ottoman sovereignty, one of Moldavia and Wallachia's economical obligations towards the Porte was to send sheep, but also sheep wool, cheese, meat and tallow in the Ottoman Empire.

90aa72df-4823-5e48-bcc0-2aa150e3f718.name: *The Suez Canal*
90aa72df-4823-5e48-bcc0-2aa150e3f718.author: Marina Minozzi
90aa72df-4823-5e48-bcc0-2aa150e3f718.keywords: Waterway; Austria; Lloyd; Assicurazioni Generali; Bourse; Adriatic; Egypt; Said; Ismail; Pasha; Ferdinand de Lesseps; Suez Canal Company; Compagnie universelle du canal maritime de Suez; vice-president; route; India; International exhibition
90aa72df-4823-5e48-bcc0-2aa150e3f718.description2: Alberto Rieger studied at the Academy of Venice thanks to the patronage of the Baron Pasquale Revoltella, who commissioned him to create the painting showing the Suez Canal, which was presented at the Exposition of Fine Arts in 1864. The artwork is meant to celebrate the most important enterprise in Revoltella’s career; he personally travelled to Suez in 1861-62 to supervise the works for the construction of the channel that he promoted. The painting was executed by studying technical maps of the ground, sketches and photographs. The result is very close to the actual conditions of the city of Cairo, the pyramids and the delta of the Nile. The artist was commissioned also an open view of the city of Trieste by Pasquale Revoltella.

9107cee6-86c6-50d5-afa3-39c67845bd31.name: Cup stand (*zarf*)
9107cee6-86c6-50d5-afa3-39c67845bd31.description: These delicate silver pieces known as *zarf* are an important part of the coffee ritual in Turkey, as they work as a protection and stand for the hot cups. We can admire those pieces as a part of the scenography in the portrait of the marquise of the Cerralbo and his daughter in Turkish costume made by Abdullah Fréres.
9107cee6-86c6-50d5-afa3-39c67845bd31.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes

9162226d-73d0-5c61-8640-f03def3fa40a.name: Pearl Trader’s Pearl Pouch
9162226d-73d0-5c61-8640-f03def3fa40a.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
9162226d-73d0-5c61-8640-f03def3fa40a.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
9162226d-73d0-5c61-8640-f03def3fa40a.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
9162226d-73d0-5c61-8640-f03def3fa40a.materials: Cotton fabric with multi-coloured, cotton embroidery threads
9162226d-73d0-5c61-8640-f03def3fa40a.description2: This colourful little bag would have contained a pearl merchant's most priced pearls. Many such bags could be found in a pearl merchant's chest, each one containing a particular grade of pearl, determined by their shape, colour and level of surface perfection.

94c59dc9-5032-599d-bcf3-18eec377e4fa.name: Velvet embroidered kaftan
94c59dc9-5032-599d-bcf3-18eec377e4fa.holder: Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires
94c59dc9-5032-599d-bcf3-18eec377e4fa.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
94c59dc9-5032-599d-bcf3-18eec377e4fa.materials: Velvet fabric, braided trimmings, silver thread with white and gold
94c59dc9-5032-599d-bcf3-18eec377e4fa.description2: This purple velvet kaftan is decorated with gold and silver braided trimmings and embroidered with silver and golden metal thread. It is fitted with mid-length sleeves embellished with a large "lyonnais" ribbon. The chest is covered by a large breastplate, split into two symmetrical halves, and adorned with large buttons of gold lace. The embroidery on the breastplate features two peacocks facing, on each side, a bowl with floral motifs. The kaftan is lined with a pale blue satinette on the outer rims with a pattern of swallows' wings sewn on. The kaftan, a particularly lavish item in the 19th century, was typically worn for marriage ceremonies, usually with calf-length trousers.

9538f776-9e52-5f16-ad4d-5fc1ca0568aa.name: Jacket
9538f776-9e52-5f16-ad4d-5fc1ca0568aa.holder: Musée Public National des Arts et Traditions Populaires

9538f776-9e52-5f16-ad4d-5fc1ca0568aa.materials: Sewing and embroidery with gold thread

954b0597-1e92-5222-bbca-efdc2174af21.name: *The Egyptian Stock Market*
954b0597-1e92-5222-bbca-efdc2174af21.keywords: The Stock Market; Securities Exchange Market; Old Alexandria
954b0597-1e92-5222-bbca-efdc2174af21.description2: An old photograph of the Egyptian Stock Market in Alexandria, one of the oldest stock markets in the world. It was established in 1899, during the time of Khedive `Abbas II, in the Muhammad `Ali square in Alexandria. The Alexandria Stock Market became a landmark in the city that frequently appears on postcards.

97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.name: Wedding dress
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.author: Huda Kilani
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.materials: Linen with silk; hand weaving, hand embroidered, natural dyes
97603dc7-78b0-567d-995d-706683438f46.description2: The main fabric of this wedding dress is linen with silk selvedge stripes, with red and yellow taffeta inserts in the sleeves and skirt; the chest panel is couched with gilt cord and yellow, green and purple silk cord, and filled with multi-coloured stain and herringbone stitches. Palestinian weavers used manual spindles to prepare the cotton and linen threads imported from Egypt. Ashkelon weavers used light vertical hand looms (*Majdalawi* looms) to produce linen fabrics, while silk fabrics were spindled, died and woven in Syria. The Jordanian economy in the late 19th and early 20th centuries relied on trade and crafts; new waves of people started to come to Jordan to participate in those industries. This object shows the diverse population composition of Jordan at that time, through personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.name: *Egyptian village scene*
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.keywords: Economy; Market; sugar cane; Egypt; local product; rural life; eating; paintings
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.materials: Water- and bodycolour over pencil, heightened with white, on blue/grey paper
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.description2: Egyptian men and women are seen here in a town or village on the Nile. In the shade of an overhanging tree a market stall displays its wares, including paper lanterns and bread. At the stall behind, sugar cane is for sale. In the background is a mosque with a white minaret, though not distinctive enough to establish the scene's locality. Pilleau had visited Egypt in the winter of 1842-43 with Lieutenant Colonel George Everest (after whom Mount Everest was named) and two other companions, on their way home from India. On his return to England he published a set of twelve coloured lithographs, Sketches in Egypt (1845), which, like the better-known publications of Wilkie, Roberts and Owen Jones in the same decade, fuelled popular interest in Egypt and the Holy Land.

99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.name: Arab / Bedouin Gun
99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.holder: Sharjah Al-Hisn Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
99c365eb-e061-5123-97ee-c6128fee870f.description2: This matchlock musket, locally made based on a European prototype, is known as 'Abu Futtila'. It is an  example of the type of weapon used from the early 18th century until as late as the early 20th century in the Arabian Peninsula. The type was typically simply stocked, but generally as with this example, fitted with an extremely high quality barrel.  The tang is stamped with a maker's mark. This gun is a good example as it retains what is possibly its original match consisting of twisted fibre cord bound with cotton and two large copper alloy tubular fittings,  probably to hold lighted sections of the match. The gun is muzzle loaded and has a  .50 calibre smoothbore barrel with a single shot firing capacity. The musket shows fine fluting and has a chiseled barrel with geometric designs and silver inlay, as well as a copper alloy mounted forward grip. The copper taper holders under the wick do not appear to be original, but this gun still has its primer pan protector.Weapons were among the most coveted and desirable, if often illicit commodities in the Arab Gulf. European weapons were mainly imported through Muscat and Bushire on the Persian coast of the Gulf, with many than copied locally.

9a890b71-5d5a-57ef-b26d-c4592e54b5ac.name: Beirut Tramway station
9a890b71-5d5a-57ef-b26d-c4592e54b5ac.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Rita El Hachem
9a890b71-5d5a-57ef-b26d-c4592e54b5ac.description2: This photograph shows the main tramway station in Beirut, located on Corniche el Nahr Street by the river in the district of Burj Hammud. It was constructed in 1906 under the command of the Ottoman government, and housed the carts and the engineering station.

9aa7bece-df44-557d-99af-6cb4118c4095.name: The yacht Makook III built by the Fratelli Orlando Company (Livorno, Italy) for the Egyptian Khedive Abbas Hilmi
9aa7bece-df44-557d-99af-6cb4118c4095.author: Daniela Tazzi
9aa7bece-df44-557d-99af-6cb4118c4095.archival: ASLi, Cantiere Navale Luigi Orlando, b. 8M2
9aa7bece-df44-557d-99af-6cb4118c4095.description2: In 1910, the Khédivé of Egypt contracted the construction of a yacht to the shipyards Cantieri Gallinari of Livorno, Italy. This company went bankrupt and its business was absorbed by the Fratelli Orlando shipyards, from Livorno as well. After improving the project, the Fratelli Orlando started building the yacht in 1913 and delivered it to the Khédivé Hilmì Abbas in May 1914.  In recognition of the high quality of work on the yacht engineer Giuseppe Orlando was granted the Ottoman decoration of the Order of Osmanieh.

9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.name: Belt
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.author: Huda Kilani
9aa9bf06-9414-5502-8c25-a49ce6269462.description2: A Circassian belt with 15 silver and niello-decorated buckles connected together to form the belt; there is a rosette shape at the end with locking mechanism and three dangling silver tassels. This belt, together with the dagger, was an accessory forming the traditional male Circassian dress. The Circassians used to carry daggers which were an essential part of the national dress. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries with which they had spiritual and religious links.

9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.name: Brass head of flagpole
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.author: Huda Kilani
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.description2: This mast, made of casted brass, bears an Arabic calligraphic decoration with the inscription "Oh God, Oh Muhammad". It is fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

9b43f3ea-5b0a-57f2-be8e-3ff0d20fe6f6.name: Beirut Port during its expansion
9b43f3ea-5b0a-57f2-be8e-3ff0d20fe6f6.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
9b43f3ea-5b0a-57f2-be8e-3ff0d20fe6f6.description2: This photograph shows the Beirut port during its expansion, which involved filling areas of sea with rock were brought along the Nahr al-Kalb railway.

9b7af802-1ae8-51cf-9420-82e3e2b1c459.name: Photograph showing Khan Antun Bey Square
9b7af802-1ae8-51cf-9420-82e3e2b1c459.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
9b7af802-1ae8-51cf-9420-82e3e2b1c459.description2: Pictured here is the Khan at Khan Antoun Bey square. The building housed trading offices on the ground and first floors and foreign consulates on the upper floors. There was also an inner courtyard used for parking the consuls' horse-drawn carriages. It was built in 1853 by Antoun Bey Najjar, a merchant who made his fortune in Constantinople. Located by the port, the construction of this building is a reflection of the increasing importance of trade between Beirut and the West following the redevelopment of the port area in 1841. The khan was an important centre for business and trade, and later served many different functions, housing foreign consulates, Ottoman administrative offices, the postal service, merchants' offices and Beirut's first bank.

9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.name: Brass head of flagpole
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.author: Huda Kilani
9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.description2: A cultic item with Arabic calligraphy mentioning God and his prophet Muhammad made of casted brass; fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized that would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.name: Dhow collection
9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.keywords: Boat; ship; dhow; pearling; fishing; trade; transportation
9c2ac3c9-ddf9-5578-9e26-fad8ec3a615c.description2: The National Museum of Qatar holds, in its collection, a fleet comprising of 14 dhows. The growing collection includes a variety of traditional dhows, with several models dating to the early 20th century, as well as more recent replicas of traditional vessels. Originating from Oman, Bahrayn, India and Qatar, among other places traditional dhows represented include *jalbut* (small to medium sized), *shuw\`i* (medium sized, once used for fishing and coastal trade), *sanbuq* (largest type in the Arabian Gulf today) and *baglah* (traditional, deep-sea dhows once used for the long – haul transport of goods.)

9dcd91c6-e5a8-5dd3-b2fb-aa1eefe94502.name: *Plan of the Suez Canal*
9dcd91c6-e5a8-5dd3-b2fb-aa1eefe94502.author: Chiara Artico

9dcd91c6-e5a8-5dd3-b2fb-aa1eefe94502.description2: This map was printed four years before the opening of the Suez Canal, in a book published in Algiers by the local Chamber of Commerce. It is evidence of the interest that the opening of the Canal aroused in North African countries other than Egypt, because of the business opportunities that it created.

9edbfb79-9af7-5f97-a619-da304ecfa112.name: Set of photos illustrating Livestock Room, Donkey Room and Sheeps and Wool Room at Fu`ad Agricultural Museum
9edbfb79-9af7-5f97-a619-da304ecfa112.dates: 16 January 1938 (Photos taken during the inauguration of the museum)
9edbfb79-9af7-5f97-a619-da304ecfa112.description2: The Fu`ad Agriculture Museum was considered the first of its kind in the Middle East and the Arab World during the 1930s. It was inaugurated during the time of King Faruq, the son of King Fu`ad, and houses a large number of collections related to agricultural and rural environments, as well as agricultural plants and animals.

a239b65c-d3b2-56bb-9598-00de8e920231.name: Bank note
a239b65c-d3b2-56bb-9598-00de8e920231.holder: Musée de la Monnaie: Banque centrale de Tunisie
a239b65c-d3b2-56bb-9598-00de8e920231.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
a239b65c-d3b2-56bb-9598-00de8e920231.description2: This 20 franc bill was first issued in 1783. It is blue and black on the front and blue on the back, and was issued by the Banque d’Algérie, which had the exclusive rights to issue notes in the Beylik of Tunis. The front of the note shows Mercury on the left and Hercules on the right. The penalty clause - article 139 - is written at the top in four lines. Beneath it we can see the inscription of the Banque d’Algérie and "20 francs". The number "20" is written in Arabic numerals on each side of the vignette with "Tunisie" written horizontally over it in black. A seated artist decorating vase is depicted on the back of the note on the left, and a harvester is on the right. The penalty clause - article 139 - is written again in six lines in a circle a the bottom. The number "20" is written in Arabic numerals on each side of the vignette.

a2684bac-db79-51f6-9e08-fdd75907b7bc.name: Choueit–'Araya Train Station
a2684bac-db79-51f6-9e08-fdd75907b7bc.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
a2684bac-db79-51f6-9e08-fdd75907b7bc.history: The train line passing through this station went from Beirut to Damascus (Baramke) via Jamhur, 'Araya, 'Aley, Bhamdun, and 'Ayn Sawfar.
a2684bac-db79-51f6-9e08-fdd75907b7bc.keywords: Commerce; Train station; Railway; Transportation; Trading
a2684bac-db79-51f6-9e08-fdd75907b7bc.description2: This train station was not only built in the French style, but also operated in the same way as French railways, demonstrating the extent of French influence on architecture and infrastructure during this period: both passenger trains and freight trains, transporting goods and raw materials across land, served this line.

a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.name: Part of a veil
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.author: Huda Kilani
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.keywords: Gold; Ottoman coins; above the nose; piece of cloth
a2f41b51-30af-503a-a290-05cb553751f2.description2: Five lines of gold ¼ Ottoman lira and other type of coins sewn together on a piece of cloth; such pieces were usually affixed above the nose on the veils, *burqu'*, of women of Beer Sheba. Fashion, local costumes and rites in the territories of Jordan and Palestine show identical elements, as this veil illustrates. It is one of the many examples of jewellery made with Ottoman coins to decorate veils and dresses. Jewellery was an important accessory for married women because pieces of jewellery constituted part of the dowry their husbands gave them for marriage. Jewellery was also a symbol of financial prestige: the more precious it was, the richer the husband’s family. Silver jewellery was the most common because only rich people could afford gold jewellery.

a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.name: Photograph of Bab Idris street
a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.description: Pictured here is Bab Idris street, leading to Bab Idris, the city's western gate and the entrance to the old town. By the time of Ahmad Bey al-Jazzar's reign (1777–1804), the city had four main gates: Bab al-Dirka to the south, Bab al-Santiya to the west, Bab al-Dabbagha to the north, and Bab al-Saraya to the east. Jazzar Pasha built fortifications between these four main gates, which was not a fortified gate. Other city gates included Bab Yaqub, also in the east, Bab Abu Nasr at Burj square, and Bab Idris. These non-military gates are reflections of the city's rapid expansion, particularly due to an increase in trade.
a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki

a3cd6343-e399-52fc-beca-9b8315cf4639.name: *Panorama of the Compagnie Transatlantique* (French Line). *The "La Ville de Rome" steamer leaving the port of Algiers via Montenard*
a3cd6343-e399-52fc-beca-9b8315cf4639.artist: Photographer: Neurdein Frères; artist: Frédéric Montenard
a3cd6343-e399-52fc-beca-9b8315cf4639.second_name: Taken from the Exposition Universelle of 1889
a3cd6343-e399-52fc-beca-9b8315cf4639.description2: The emergence of steam boats in the 19th century allowed important maritime trade relationships to develop. In 1855, the Pereire brothers adopted this new method of transport and founded the Compagnie Générale Transatlantique (The French Line). The first line built served New York. In the 1880s the company then established an important line from Marseille to North Africa, which consisted of a 12-steamer strong fleet, the "sister ships" of the "Ville de Rome", which was first put into use in 1881. In March 1889, the "Ville de Rome" was run aground and washed up on the shores of Menorca. The passengers were evacuated in time, but the storm caused the wreck of the ship to break in two.

a4505a95-37ac-56ac-a759-301f36d101f1.name: Ottoman coin – 10 Kurush 1876
a4505a95-37ac-56ac-a759-301f36d101f1.description2: After Moldavia and Wallachia became vassals of the Ottoman Empire, their rulers lost the right to struck coins. Therefore, commercial exchanges were done using foreign coins, the most widely  circulated being Ottoman coinage. Things changed in the second half of the 19th century when national coins were issued in the United Principalities starting with 1867.

a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.name: Water jug
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.author: Huda Kilani
a46e70b6-0a07-57b9-ad2a-d974179b2424.description2: A copper circular-shaped ewer with a very narrow neck, arched handle and strait long nozzle, used in mosques of Jordan and Palestine to wash before praying. This is another example of how the same objects, traditions, and activities were common in territories that now belong to different Arab states. In the late 19th century and early 20th century, there were still no boundaries between the Arab states and this – together with the lack of geographical barriers – made population movements, nomadism and migration a common factor influencing the everyday life and exchanges in the local society. The local economy, which relied heavily on trade and crafts, depended also on travel and migration in order to sell products or find markets for craft products.

a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.name: *The Coffee Shop*
a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
a57ada78-0cee-53e5-9161-c701a353df82.description2: Coffee shops in the Near and Middle East were regular meeting places for men, who could while away hours chatting, playing domino, smoking and – crucially if dangerously – talking politics. In early 20th century Cairo as elsewhere, spedific cafes became important hubs for social and political discourse.This painting shows a traditional Near Eastern street café. Customers are sitting on long benches in front of its wooden openwork facade, A waiter with a red fez carries a brass coffee pot (dallah) and a tray. Behind him, through the wooden screen, the preparation area, in which the coffee is made, can just be seen on the left. A man wearing a white turban and blue gown, perhaps the proprietor, looks out on the right. All present are captivated by a carpet seller, who is standing in front of the cafe, offering up his wares.

a7135e6b-1b7e-5ddf-9568-b2daa5ac8d45.name: Louis Pasteur's work on silkworm illnesses. *Healthy Worms*
a7135e6b-1b7e-5ddf-9568-b2daa5ac8d45.description2: Silkworm farming developed in both France and Italy from the 15th century. Over-intensive farming caused the spread of various silkworm-based illnesses in the mid-19th century. Louis Pasteur, the famous scientist known for his work on the rabies vaccine amongst other things, was called on to find a cure. In 1870 he published *Une Étude sur la Maladie des Vers à Soie*, in which he proposed the use of various preventive methods, which proved effective. Pictured here is an illustration of silkworms immune to illness.

a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.name: 'Casa del Mar' Fortress
a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.history: Tarfaya became a British airmail postal centre in 1882. In 1889, Scottish entrepreneur Donald Mackenzie persuaded the head of Sous, Muhammad Bayruk, to allow him to establish a trading post on Tarfaya strip (also known as Cape Juby strip), which was about three kilometres wide by 12 km long. Mackenzie built the factory/trading post and named it Port Victoria, which he managed through his own North-West Africa Company. Under the Spanish Protectorate the name was changed to Casa Del Mar (House of the Sea).
a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.keywords: Caravan; caravan routes; trade; economy; commerce; port; traditional port; sea routes; maritime routes; traditional routes; trading hubs; trading route; strategical port; strategical hub; modernisation; industrialisation; Moroccan ports; Islamic city; changes in urban space; Moroccan city; foreign companies; Nort West Africa; British in Morocco; postal services; British postal service; factory; industrialists; industrial architecture; military architecture; British architects; British architects in Morocco; fortress; Spanish in Morocco
a7ce06ce-7dc4-5296-b742-d917fdbbf2c7.description2: At the end of the 19th century, Scottish entrepreneur Donald Mackenzie persuaded the Governor of Sous, Muhammad Bayruk, to cede him a strip of land roughly three kilometres wide and 12km long on which to establish a trading post. It was known as Tarfaya strip or the Cape Juby strip. On it, Mackenzie built Port Victoria, a trading post/factory, which he managed through his own North-West Africa Company, hoping to capture a portion of the caravan trade. The reinforced stone buttressed building of two floors covers an area of 1,200m².

a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.name: Decanter (one of a set of three)
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.type: Furniture and decorative objects; vessel; glasswork
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.holder: Shangri La, Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.provenance: Europe, made for export to Iran
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.keywords: decanter; glass; beads; decoupage; Qajar; Nasr al-Din Shah; Europe; portrait
a8c2cd08-42f5-5b60-8ef5-5d255e20c9a4.description2: During the nineteenth century, European centres of glass production, particularly those in France and Bohemia, created Islamic-style works of art to be exported to countries like Egypt, Syria, Iran, and India. The DDFIA collection includes several examples of such European glass. This bottle – one in a set of three – was certainly produced for an Iranian recipient, for it features portraits of the Qajar shah Nasr al-Din (r. 1848–96). Purchased in 1959.

a9007630-d81f-5724-87ad-6fc202c954e3.name: Gufas (Quffas) on the Tigris at Baghdad
a9007630-d81f-5724-87ad-6fc202c954e3.description2: This stereoview by the Keystone company (a reprint from an older negative) was part of a popular box-set of images about Mesopotamia. They were sold across Europe. The text on the reverse contains description of the geography, architecture (explanation of minarets, lament at the absence of fine buildings through devastation of the city by fire, habit of wealthy to live in unpretentious houses to avoid the attention of the Turkish taxman) and history, plus brief caption in half a dozen languages.

abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.name: Café du Marabout in the Souk Ettrouk
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.archival: Copied from a drawing by Sir Grenville Temple, published in his book The Shores and Islands of the Mediterranean in London in 1840, this drawing was taken from Chelli Zouhir, La Tunisie au Rythme des Estampes du Xve au XIXe siecle (Tunis, ed. Tunis Carthage: 1992), p. 65, fig. 25.
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.description2: This copy of a beautiful watercolour from Charles Lallemand's book Tunis et ses Environs shows the Café el-Mourabit in the Turkish souk, also known as the tailors' souk, in the Tunis medina near the Zaytuna Mosque. The café was especially known for its Andalusian architecture. The customers sit on mats sipping coffee, leaning on archways and pillars.

ad246261-371b-52ce-a11b-7790d61625de.name: Al-Hisn Fort
ad246261-371b-52ce-a11b-7790d61625de.holder: Sharjah Museums Authority / Sharjah Heritage Directorate
ad246261-371b-52ce-a11b-7790d61625de.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
ad246261-371b-52ce-a11b-7790d61625de.notice: Please note that this is an unedited database entry and that it may contain grammatical errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are working to raise the funds required to complete the editing of the database; should you wish to contribute please visit our [Support page](https://www.museumwnf.org/atrium_support.php).
ad246261-371b-52ce-a11b-7790d61625de.description2: The first fort at Sharjah town was destroyed by the British in 1819-20. Under Shaikh Sultan bin Saqr II al-Qasimi a new fort was built 1823/4. From sources we can assume that the original fort was of traditional square one-storey design with tall corner towers and an inner courtyard. Its most unusual element was the design of its al-Mhalousa tower, *mhalous* meaning 'twisted' in Arabic. Originally, Sharjah's fort, known as *al-Hisn*, was built onto the desert side of the previously existing town wall and incorporated a round tower known as *al-Kabs*. The fort served as the residence of the ruling Qasimi family until the early 14th/20th century. In 1970 it was partially demolished to make way for urban development, but several key parts, including the so-called *al-Kabs* tower on its northwestern side, survived. The current fort – a reconstruction and a museum – stands as a reminder to an important building of crucial importance to Sharjah's history, witnessing key political, social, commercial and military events in its history.

ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.name: *Suq al-Hamidiyya, Damascus*
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.author: Stefan Weber
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.second_name: Covered market constructed in the shape of an arcade turning it to the worldwide longest arcade of the fin de siecle
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.description2: The Suq al-Hamidiyya, built in 1886 and 1894, is by far the biggest and most famous suq in Damascus. This bazaar street also links the two most important historic buildings, the Umayyad Mosque and the Citadel. It was built along its western section by incorporating earlier structures, whereas the eastern part of the street was a completely new construction cutting through the existing buildings. The commercial thoroughfare is 450 metres long and 8.70 to 9.90 metres wide, its enormous size and the high standard of its execution accentuate new design principles. So in various respects, this suq is a very interesting example of structural change in a traditional commercial centre.

aea6e497-0dd2-52bd-b31b-8f9ac8b8e29c.description: A photograph depicting workers at the Arms Factory in Fez.

aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.name: *A Greek lady of Smyrna*
aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.author: Delivorrias, Fotopoulos 1997, 503, fig. 888 (Elisabeth Karanopoulou)
aee0c11d-b05a-5082-9164-78ab982f4882.description2: The picture probably depicts a bride before being bedecked. Her outfit-one of the two customary types of urban bridal costume during the Ottoman period- consists of one or two pairs of pantaloons, a diaphanous selvedged chemise and a dress with tightly buttoned long sleeves and a sash worn low on the hips. Her overcoat is trimmed with fur, has wide pointed sleeves and the dress appears to have been hitched up, revealing the bottom of the pantaloons. Among the various testimonies bequeathed to us by the foreign artist-travelers who visited Greece in the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries, the depictions of costumes are particularly important. The imaginative combination of the various garments and accessories that make up the Greek costume and the wealth of jewellery fascinated foreign travellers, who recorded them pictorially, often with a dubitable degree of accuracy.

en: Delivorrias, Angelos, and Fotopoulos, Dionisis, *Greece at the Benaki Museum*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1997.

b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.name: Steam engine building
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.holder: Prussian Palaces (Stiftung Preussische Schlösser und Gärten Berlin Brandenburg)
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.history:
In October 1842 the steam engine in the "Mosque," which could reach 81.4 horsepower, was inaugurated, allowing jets of water from the great fountain in front of Sanssouci Palace to rise to an impressive 38 meters. By possessing what was the most powerful machine in Prussia at the time, built by the young entrepreneur August Borsig, King Frederick William IV hoped to compete with the technical supremacy of England.  
Although today's supply of water to the fountains in Sanssouci Park is provided by means of modern electrical pumps, a visit to the "Mosque" allows the visitor to experience a technical marvel from days past that is still in operation.
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.keywords: Moorish style; Romanticism; Sanssouci; Potsdam; exoticism; steam engine; steam pumping; Frederick William IV; gardens
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.description2: The Steam Engine Building, located on a bay of the Havel River called the Neustädter Havelbucht, is at once the most charming as well as the most exotic building in Potsdam. Frederick William IV, the "Romantic on the throne," had it built by Ludwig Persius from 1841-1843, "in the style of the Turkish mosques, with a minaret as a smokestack." The building, which could still be seen at that time from Sanssouci Palace, added a picturesque architectural accent to the Potsdam cultural landscape.

b2525f86-10f4-5e6f-b558-0f92275571e7.name: Sword with scabbard
b2525f86-10f4-5e6f-b558-0f92275571e7.description: A sword and scabbard decorated with geometric and floral motifs and crafted in southern Morocco in the 19th century. Sword blades were imported from Europe, especially from Toledo in Spain, or from Damascus in Syria.

b3139452-a18c-5578-a8f9-65f5a88d9fe0.name: A treaty between the Regency of Tunis and the Grand Duke of Tuscany, concerning the jurisdiction over Tuscan Jews who migrated to Tunisia
b3139452-a18c-5578-a8f9-65f5a88d9fe0.author: Loredana Maccabruni
b3139452-a18c-5578-a8f9-65f5a88d9fe0.archival: ASFi, Trattati Internazionali, CXCII [192]: “Modificazione del Trattato commerciale fatto colla Reggenza di Tunisi nel 1822 relativamente agli Israeliti”
b3139452-a18c-5578-a8f9-65f5a88d9fe0.description2:
Treaty of one article, in Italian and Arabic, signed by the Tuscan Consul Enrico Nyssen and by the Bey Ahmed Bascià, sealed with a wax seal of the Consulate General of Tuscany, and ratified by the Grand Duke of Tuscany Leopold the II on 29 January 1847.  
This treaty modified the 1822 treaty between the two countries which had given to the Jews from Livorno the same status of Tunisian Jews (placing them under the Beys' jurisdiction). According to this new treaty, the Tuscan Jews who had moved to Tunisia (or would move to Tunisia in the future) and registered in the Tuscan Consulate, were placed under Tuscan jurisdiction and protection. Such provision did not apply to the so-called “Grana” Jews who had moved to Tunisia from Livorno (Tuscany) in the late 17th century.

b4dc43ea-b3d1-58c6-bc57-9f2f74291cc6.name: Medal – Semi-centenary of the European Commission of the Danube
b4dc43ea-b3d1-58c6-bc57-9f2f74291cc6.description2:
In 1856, the treaty of Paris, signed on 30 March, internationalized the Danube and established the European Commission of the Danube, an inter-state institution (comprising delegates of Austria, France, Great Britain, Prussia, Sardinia and Russia) that had to ensure and facilitate navigation at the mouths of the river.  
Issued on the 50th anniversary of the Commission, this medal was designed by O. Patey. On the obverse is depicted the god Danubius, holding a trident in his left hand and lying by the Danube, with his elbow on a stone pipe from which water flows into the river. On the edge is inscribed “Commission Européenne du Danube. On the reverse “1856-1906” is engraved inside a wreath of oak and laurel leaves. Above there is the inscription: “Article 16 du Traite de Paris du 30 Mars 1856”.

b5f42e1e-ecb3-55b6-8189-981be88d8626.name: National loan 1920. *Banque National d'Escompte de Paris… National loan, 1920, 6%... Sign up for a loan and save in the future…*
b5f42e1e-ecb3-55b6-8189-981be88d8626.description2: As the First World War was proving longer and more costly than predicted, the French government took out two loans in 1915 and in 1918 to fund weaponry and other wartime expenses. After the war, more loans were taken out to rebuild the country. Posters with simple messages were used to persuade the population that these loans were beneficial to the country, and would have huge returns. We can see on this poster, for example, a French cockerel standing on a horn, a symbol of abundance, from which money is overflowing.

b632cf54-9527-5f85-9a5a-5d9445c932a8.name: Indian Rupee of Empress Victoria (Um al-Bint)
b632cf54-9527-5f85-9a5a-5d9445c932a8.holder: Sharjah Heritage Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
b632cf54-9527-5f85-9a5a-5d9445c932a8.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
b632cf54-9527-5f85-9a5a-5d9445c932a8.description2: This silver coin represents one Indian rupee, minted in 1877. Regal issues of the Indian rupee had begun in 1862, bearing the portrait of Queen Victoria, but Indian Rupees had already been used in the Gulf during the mid 19th century, issued by the British East India Company. The currency began circulating in the region as a result of the pearl trade and the gold exchange between local and Indian merchants. Indian rupees were the main currency used in the Trucial States up until 1966.

b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.name: Gospel cover of Dorotheos Proios from Edirne
b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.author: Ballian 1992, 86-7, no.46
b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.description2: The gospel comes from Adrianople, but a handwritten note on the second page notes that: "…it was crafted and decorated here in Smyrna". From around the mid-eighteenth century Smyrna was the second most important port of the Ottoman Empire, and an important part of its economic life was in the hands of Greeks. The “Frankish quarter” and the preponderance of large-scale, foreign trade gave o cosmopolitan air to Smyrniot society. There is strong western European influence on this impressive silver cover made for Dorotheos Proios. Scrolled cartouches, thronging garlands of roses and conch shells in high relief make it a triumph of Rococo art, at least after the fashion in which it was understood in the Ottoman Empire. Smyrna was an important centre of silver production, but the designs were in general circulation and compositions were put together to fit the circumstances.

en: Ballian, Anna, *Treasures from the Greek Communities of Asia Minor and Eastern Thrace. Collections from the Benaki Museum*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1992.

b660b1ab-20b9-54c4-8225-fc35360b345d.description2:

However, the most important monetary event took place in 1898, when Khedive \`Abbas Hilmi II granted a franchise to Raphael Suares to establish the National Bank of Egypt. This franchise gave him the right to produce securities that were accepted to pay domanial money, and the right to cash this money as gold upon demand.

b94c1c17-a6e6-5cac-b93a-a36603dd4d29.description2: In the beginning of the 20th century, traditional commerce activities still coexisted alongside newer, modern commercial transport. baca824e-062d-5426-b385-13a5074e8755.description2: In 1762, Muslims living in Livorno were granted a plot of land outside the city walls, near the beach, to build a graveyard (highlighted in green in the lithography). The graveyard remained in use until the second half of the 19th century. A Muslim graveyard existed in Livorno even before the 18th century. A significant Muslim community lived in town. Its first members were captives taken to Italy as slaves. Muslim traders settled in town as well. In 1856, the graveyard was enlarged and surrounded by walls. In 1872 it was demolished to build a road and some of the graves were moved to the city graveyard.

bc4af44a-740c-54ce-806a-021695934601.name: Yıldız Ceramic vase
bc4af44a-740c-54ce-806a-021695934601.description2: Sultan Abdülhamid II founded in 1891 the *Yıldız Çini Fabrika-i Hümâyûnu* (Yıldız Royal Tile Factory) in the garden of Yıldız Palace in order to revive Turkish tile art and give it a new direction and momentum. Vases, hanging wall plates and many sorts of daily-use wares were produced in the factory, including writing and dinner table utensils, card plates, lidded bowls, pans, *aşure* (a kind of dessert) trays, sugar bowls, tea and coffee cups. The vase has yellow covers and two handles. There is a landscape of a tree and a house near the water on the vase.

Hollow domes and welded reliefs with locking mechanism. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom.  
The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for these purposes. bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th century

bd591c95-bb06-5105-b1bd-b95187ad7a88.description2: Luigi Rey was the son of Italian immigrants Giuseppe Rey (1808-1897), of Piedmont and Adelaide Baldacci, of Tuscany. In 1836, Giuseppe Rey was dispatched to Tunis by his employer, a construction company from Genoa, to work in the Bardo Palace (the official residence of the Bey of Tunis). After completing the contract Giuseppe decided to stay in Tunisia, where he continued to work at the service of the Bey. Together with his three children (Luigi, Antonio and Pio), Giuseppe Rey set up a construction company that continued after his death. Predominantly with his brothers but at times on his own, Luigi Rey built a variety of private and public edifices, including the Tunisia Palace Hotel (designed by architect Resplandy).

bd9ac0b4-17dd-5d2a-86a5-baadbae9f621.description2: Jeweller’s wooden box to keep tools such as hand drills, punctures and screws, and soldering iron clumps. This tool box belonged to an Armenian jeweller whose family left their country during the First World War and settled in Jerusalem. The jeweller then moved to Amman and settled there in 1948. The Armenians were well known as skilled craftsmen and jewellers. The owner of this box worked as a jeweller since the 1950's, using his tool box until his death. The tool box demonstrates the relationship between different waves of migration and the variegated demographic composition of the Jordanians.
