be90f64f-96f3-5dda-8345-68adf8244431.description2: Frédéric Alexianu (aka F. Hugo d'Alesi) was a painter who quickly became specialised in advertisement posters for different kinds of transports, and in educational maps. This poster, aimed at primary school children, uses the example of Marseille to illustrate a trading port. The artist draws attention to the different commercial activities undertaken here, in addition to the transport of passengers on an ocean liner. The port of Marseille was the most important Mediterranean port in France, as it facilitated a great number of commercial exchanges with the French colonies in North Africa.

The mortar is highly decorated with floral and geometric designs. After roasting the coffee beans, the local Bedouins use these to grind the beans. The sound of grinding functions as an invitation to others to come and chat while enjoying freshly prepared coffee.

c1018611-912b-5af9-adeb-c669911527d4.description2: This rare copper alloy coin, known as 'Madhrouf Al Qawasim and weighing around 6.5 grams in weight, was minted in the trading port of Lanja (Linga) on the Persian coast of the Gulf in 1247 H/ 1831 CE.  In the 12th/18th and early 13th/ early 19th century, Lanja belonged to the extensive territories on both sides of the Gulf held by the Al Qawasim, and coins like this were used throughout the regions ruled by the Qawasim family at the time, including their main centres in Sharjah, Ras al Khaimah, Kalba, Khor Fakkan and Diba.

c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.name: Three
c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
c120b65a-cd13-5c60-a28b-463b99dc6f57.description2: These water pipes, or *araghil* (sing. *arghile*), is made of translucent glass painted with floral patterns in pale colours. The *araghil* have three main parts: first, you have a bowl for the coals sitting on top of a metal plate. Under this is the body of the *arghile*, which can come in a variety of shapes and sizes, and consists of a gasket and water jar. Connected to the main body is a pipe for smoking. The *arghile* originated in Persia and later became popular in 17th century Turkey, used by the Ottoman elite as a status symbol. The water pipe became hugely popular, and in 1841 even sparked a diplomatic crisis between France and the Ottoman Empire. However, although it remains popular in the modern Middle East, it was largely replaced by cigarettes in the 20th century. The *arghile* woks by vaporizing a flavoured tobacco called *shisha*, which is passed through water and then inhaled. Depending on their placement, the coals can either be used to boil the water and thus create water vapour, or to produce smoke by burning the tobacco. These *araghil* were used by Ottoman officials in 19th century Lebanon.

Among the landmarks illustrated and described, as well as the new Royal Stock Exchange, is the Crystal Palace, the site of the Universal Exhibition (the Great Exhibition) of 1851.

cab1d1b6-5bd0-5d68-aaf4-36e8d7c863e4.name: *View of Smyrna*
cab1d1b6-5bd0-5d68-aaf4-36e8d7c863e4.author: Papastratos 1990, vol. 2, 578-79, figs. 617-18; Delivorrias, Fotopoulos 1997, 508-9, figs. 900-901
cab1d1b6-5bd0-5d68-aaf4-36e8d7c863e4.description2: Both this print and the *View of Constantinople* are based on earlier Western ones, which have been assimilated into the distinctive Athonite topographical style. They are exceptions to the corpus of Athonite prints, since they are of secular subjects. The printmaker was, indeed, active outside Athos, where he executed nonreligious commissions. The subjects relate to the tradition of topographical murals depicting important commercial and cultural centers of the day that decorated the mansions of wealthy merchants by the mid-eighteenth century. Kaldis aimed to supply a wider public with inexpensive works of a decorative nature. The activity of merchants from Lesbos at Smyrna, Constantinople, and the Black Sea on the one hand justified the choice of subject and, on the other, provided the appropriate network in which the multiple printed works could circulate. In order to attract the largest possible clientele, the view is coloured.

cc3eb98f-be74-5f38-85da-465d5c36d52e.description2: A rectangular piece of Syrian silk cloth (*atlas*) with a small piece of coloured cotton cloth on the front on two sides. There is a line of Ottoman coins sewn together with three tassels dangling at the end with different stones. Silver was the most common jewellery, given by the groom to the bride as dowry. The use of Ottoman coins as pieces of jewellery – shown by women to friends and relatives – was an indirect reference to the financial status of their husbands. Silk was imported from Syria. Its trade in the Syro-Palestinian area was common because of the lack of geographical and political boundaries; some cities were like twins because of their close proximity and exchange of trade goods and business.

ccd55fea-ff71-54b1-802d-9b86aa9adc8d.name: Records of the tests and of the delivery of the yacht Makook III built by the Fratelli Orlando Company (Livorno, Italy) for the Egyptian Khedive Abbas Hilmi

ccd55fea-ff71-54b1-802d-9b86aa9adc8d.archival: ASLi, Cantiere Navale Luigi Orlando, b. 8M2
ccd55fea-ff71-54b1-802d-9b86aa9adc8d.description2: In 1910, the Khédivé of Egypt contracted the construction of a yacht to the shipyards Cantieri Gallinari of Livorno, Italy. This company went bankrupt and its business was absorbed by the Fratelli Orlando shipyards, also from Livorno. After improving the project, the Fratelli Orlando started building the yacht in 1913 and delivered it to the Khédivé Hilmì Abbas in May 1914. In recognition of the high quality of work on the yacht engineer Giuseppe Orlando was granted the Ottoman decoration of the Order of Osmanieh.

d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.name: *The Grand Bazaar Istanbul*
d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
d33416a4-0a7d-53e7-981b-69aa3e40b575.description2: This painting provides a fascinating insight into the activities within the Grand Bazaar of Istanbul during the 19th century CE. First built in the 15th century, its importance had declined somewhat in the 19th century, as non-Muslim merchants increasingly established independent shops in the European quarters of Istanbul rather than staying in the ‘outdated’ bazaar. Nevertheless, in 1890, there were still well over 4000 shops in the Bazaar. This image provides much detail about the appearance of traditional merchants and shops. Men, including some soldiers in European-style uniforms, and women in colourful local dress can be seen milling about the bazaar, their costume revealing important details about their ethnicity, profession and social status.

d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.name: Pearl Diver’s Finger Protectors
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.type: 15 leather finger protectors with cotton bag
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.dimensions: The finger protectors length around 40 mm, width c. 20 mm; the bag c. 250 x 200 mm
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.description2: These finger guards are known as khabt (pl. khabta). They were an essential part of a pearl-diver's equipment, as they protected his finger tips from the sharp oyster shells and other unexpected dangerous objects the pearl-diver might brush his fingers against while searching the murky seabed. Much of his work had to rely on touch, as visibility was minimal and few dangers could be anticipated by sight alone. When not used, the finger guards were kept in a container filled with water to keep them supple.

d5146f7c-a989-5ed0-8084-92511311bc67.name: An insurance policy by the company Compagnia Affricana (based in Trieste), for the merchandise transported by the Tuscan brigantine *Otello*, from Alexandria (Egypt) to Livorno (Italy)

d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.name: *Shipping at Constantinople*
d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
d51c4926-dec8-5d72-9ed4-34a107dddbd4.description2: Istanbul’s geographic position between Europe and Asia and on the only sea route that connects the Black Sea with the Mediterranean gave Istanbul great strategic importance. The control of the Bosphorus, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Marmara, was repeatedly at stake in the 19th and early 20th centuries. This 1910 watercolour gives a wonderful impression of the bustling shipping and trading activities on the waters surrounding the city of Constantinople at the time. The view is taken from the Galata side of the city, looking across the Golden Horn towards its historic heart, dominated by imperial Suleymaniye mosque on the right and Bayezid tower in the centre. The Galata bridge, in its third incarnation as completed by the British firm G. Wells in 1875, can be seen connecting the two shores. Sailing boats like those seen here brought in wheat, spices and wood. The emergence of the steamship later in the century lead to enormous increase in the speed and volume of commodities shipped to Constantinople.

dbf4dc13-3f6b-5da9-bf05-cfabe7876ad3.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
dbf4dc13-3f6b-5da9-bf05-cfabe7876ad3.author: Huda Kilani
dbf4dc13-3f6b-5da9-bf05-cfabe7876ad3.description2: A silver circular disk with inherent decorations in the carving, and prominent dome above; chains dangling with oval shapes at the end. With two different length. This ornament was placed on the top of a high hat worn by al-Druze (Druse) women. Silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and the demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.name: Dress
ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.description2: Long black silk dress (*malas*), narrow at the waist, wide at the bottom, embroidered with cross-stitch dark blue and red on the chest and on the front side, worn by women of the al-Druze tribes, with a shirt underneath. This object illustrates the variegated composition and the demographic changes of the Jordan population in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also shows how the different populations brought with them their fashion, costumes and rites which contributed to the multifaceted social and cultural heritage of Jordan. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to northeast Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

dde582f0-5bed-53bd-adaa-91e404fab4de.name: Orfella. The kaimacan Mohàmmed-el-Jesir [Qaimaqan Muhammad al-Jazir] and Notables Observe Studies on Subterranean Water of Wadi Beni Ulid Requested from the Italian Mission

dde582f0-5bed-53bd-adaa-91e404fab4de.description2: In 1911, right before the beginning of Italy’s colonial war in Libya, an expert in sulphur mining, Ignazio Sanfilippo, headed a mission to Libya to look for mineral resources (in particular, for sulphur mines). The mission was sponsored by the Libyan branch of the Banca di Roma (one of the most important Italian banks, which supported Italian colonial expansion in Libya), and it was encouraged by the Italian government. In 1910, Sanfilippo had already headed another Italian mission to Libya. He had been secretly charged by the Minister of Foreign Affairs to look for sulphur mines and the Banca di Roma had helped organising the mission.

dfc4cc0b-d5f3-5aa9-a482-5dd72c63bdf8.keywords: Trade; route; port; Great Britain; India; coffee; Red Sea; Yemen; Mocha; British settlement on the route to India; communication; telegraph; telegraph between ports; Suez Canal; pilgrimage; Makka; Arab Peninsula; Holy places
dfc4cc0b-d5f3-5aa9-a482-5dd72c63bdf8.description2:
*The Red Sea Pilot* included sailing indications and directions for navigation from the Suez Canal to the strait of Bab el-Mandeb, including Aqaba, Jeddah and the coast of Hijaz as far as Aden.  
  
Trading activity (especially in grain) between the two coasts of the Red Sea and the maritime traffic after the opening of the Suez Canal were fundamental economic activities, hence the importance of reliable knowledge of navigation routes, sailing directions, climate, winds and currents. In addition to the local ships used to carry pilgrims to Mecca and for trading activity, European ships crossed the Red Sea. The book also provides information about the main ports and their facilities. For example, it states that the telegraph had been installed from Suez to Swakin and from Swakin to Jeddah, and that there was telegraph communication between Aden, Suez, Bombay and the Cape of Good Hope.

dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.name: Dress
dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.keywords: Dress; machine embroidery; patterns; custmes and rites; Ottoman coins
dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.materials: Chinese cotton, silver coins; machine weaving, machine embroidery
dfd2eeea-301b-506a-85f9-f9ad927ce8f2.description2: Women's costumes of the central regions of Jordan are characterized by length, dark colours, light vertical strips of embroidery and very long sleeves. This black and blue dress has a very loose fitting, open chest and long flared sleeves pulled over a head band. The length of the dress was adjusted to the height of the woman by a sash. Wide at the bottom, it is decorated horizontally with blue cotton stripes and vertically with embroidery lines and Ottoman coins. The traditional costumes reflect the variegated population composition and demographic changes of the late 19th century-early 20th century Jordanian territory, when new waves of people arrived and settled for the purpose of trades and crafts. Craft was not limited to the everyday life and the profits from crafts were a source of income.

dff63501-6388-5281-9baf-bb1a3d253e7f.description2: Four pieces of wood formed into a rectangular shape; the top and bottom are covered with animal skin and joined with goat’s intestines. The rababa is played with a bow consisting of an arched stick with horse hair. The rababa is a musical instrument widely used in the Bedouin tradition. Music played in communal setting is an essential part of the traditions in Bedouin communities for leisure at communal gatherings.

e06ef895-2b01-5e26-b048-45ebf4f4ecc7.name: Palace of Monserrate
e06ef895-2b01-5e26-b048-45ebf4f4ecc7.holder: Sintra Parks Monte da Lua, Conservation Company
e06ef895-2b01-5e26-b048-45ebf4f4ecc7.author: Carlos Marques, Cristina Correia
e06ef895-2b01-5e26-b048-45ebf4f4ecc7.history: The Monserrate estate, known as the Quinta da Boa Vista,  goes back to the 16th century, belonging to the Royal All Saints Hospital as a source of revenue. The name Monserrate comes from the 1540 chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Montserrat. Formerly owned  by Beckford’s, then by the Melo e Castro family, in 1841, at the end of his grand tour, Francis Cook stops in Lisbon and marries the daughter of an English merchant. He discovers Sintra during his honeymoon and fascinated by Monserrate, manages to purchase it and starts its rehabilitation. The ensemble belonged to the Cook family until 1929. In 1947, it is sold to antiques dealer Saul Sárraga who sells in auction the contents of the palace and tries to divide the estate leading to the acquisition by the Portuguese State, in 1949.
e06ef895-2b01-5e26-b048-45ebf4f4ecc7.keywords: Sintra; Romanticism; William Beckford; Neo-Moorish; Eclecticism
e06ef895-2b01-5e26-b048-45ebf4f4ecc7.architects: Architect: James Thomas Knowles; Landscape architect: William Colebrooke Stockdale; Master gardener: Francis James Burt
e06ef895-2b01-5e26-b048-45ebf4f4ecc7.description2:
The Palace of Monserrate is a key example of Portuguese romanticism, due to its eclecticism blending Venetian Gothic influences with those of India and the Moors. The building is a landmark in the landscape, with its distinctive profile punctuated by three towers, perfectly framed with the surrounding gardens.  
The former building’s volumetry, two cylindrical turrets, horizontal galleries and a square-based central turret, the windows with Gothic arches are combined to the 19th century influences of Venetian palaces and a decorative composition of vegetative motifs. The stuccoes of the Corridor of the palace of Monserrate are inspired by the ones of Alhambra Palace in Granada whereby the several columns is thought to recall those of the Hypostyle Hall of the Cordova Mosque.

e3bfc26f-8bee-5688-a4c2-f5a33020ddd2.name: Maria Theresa Dollar
e3bfc26f-8bee-5688-a4c2-f5a33020ddd2.holder: Sharjah Heritage Museum/ Sharjah Museums Department

e3bfc26f-8bee-5688-a4c2-f5a33020ddd2.description2: This large silver coin is known as the Maria Theresia Dollar. It shows a portrait of the Austrian Empress Maria Theresia on the obverse and the Imperial double-headed eagle of the Habsburgs on the reverse. Originally minted in 1741, the Austrian Maria Theresia dollar became extremely important for Levant trade and was eventually  declared official trade coinage in 1857, one year before it ceased as currency in Austria itself. In the Arab peninsula, and especially in the lower Gulf and Oman, it remained the favoured currency until 1920, highly regarded for its high silver content. Those involved in the pearling trade, including captains of the pearling ships plying the Gulf, preferred to receive their money in Maria Theresia Dollars.

e42495ba-7c27-5b68-b246-c0dc7389d3b6.description2: The naval Port of Alexandria is the most important port in Egypt in terms of the volume of trade transactions that go through it. The Port of Alexandria handles almost 60 per cent of Egypt’s external trade.

e4c6d454-9f18-5654-bdf6-7ba2ce34e089.name: *Map of the desert between the Nile and the Red Sea, including Mount Zabara \[…\] and the remains of the ancient trade route between Egypt and India*
e4c6d454-9f18-5654-bdf6-7ba2ce34e089.artist: Author: Frédéric Cailliaud; cartographer: Edme-François Jomard; engraver: Alexandre Blondeau
e4c6d454-9f18-5654-bdf6-7ba2ce34e089.second_name: Drawn according to M. Caillaud's itinerary, by M. Jomard, and engraved by M. Blondeau.
e4c6d454-9f18-5654-bdf6-7ba2ce34e089.description2: The explorer and naturalist Frédéric Cailliaud made significant contributions to the birth of Egyptology thanks to the hieroglyphic tracings he made during his two trips to Egypt (1815–1818; 1819–1822). Muhammad 'Ali Pasha had tasked him with exploring the banks of the Nile and Nubia, where he discovered the monuments and emerald mines of Mount Zabara, and took several tracings from them, which he brought back to France with him. His observations were compiled and published by E.F. Jomard as a sequel to *l'Expedition d'Egypte*.

e5e89b24-3038-55eb-a80c-b9bb6fb8a999.name: A rare photo of the inauguration of the Luxor–Aswan Railway Line
e5e89b24-3038-55eb-a80c-b9bb6fb8a999.keywords: Land Roads; Adly Yakan Pasha; Railway Lines; Luxor; Aswan
e5e89b24-3038-55eb-a80c-b9bb6fb8a999.description2: The Honour Guard lining up to receive the guests of the inauguration of the Luxor–Aswan railway line at the Shalal Station in 1926. One of the rare photos of the inauguration of the Luxor–Aswan railway line, with `Adli Yakan Pasha; Muhammad Najib al-Gharabli Pasha; Husayn Rushdi Pasha; Tharwat Pasha; Fathallah Barakat Pasha; Morkos Hanna Pasha; al-Dagwi Bek, director of Aswan; and Mahmud Shakir Bek, deputy undersecretary of the Ministry of Transportation in attendance, in 1926.

e6cf18df-e25d-5b11-980d-12274cacd23c.name: Syrian Kingdom dinar
e6cf18df-e25d-5b11-980d-12274cacd23c.description: In March 8, 1920 the general Syrian congress met in Damascus and declared Syria and Palestine independent, with Faisal as king of the Arab Kingdom of Syria and Palestine. On that occasion a gold dinar was struck. In obverse field is “Faisal al-Awwal” written in Divan Jali script, surrounded by a wreath, on top seven pointed stars and the date 1338 (AH) below, all are within a circle of dots. On the reverse, a seven-pointed star and a shield surmounted by a crown and leaning on a wreath, with the date 1920 below. The marginal legend has the word "dinar" on the right, "*al-mamlaka*" on the top and "*al-suriya*" on the left, all are within a circle of dots. It is considered a rare coin.
e6cf18df-e25d-5b11-980d-12274cacd23c.author: Aida Naghawi
e6cf18df-e25d-5b11-980d-12274cacd23c.keywords: Damascus; Faisal al-Awwal; united Kingdom of Syria and Palestine; gold; coin; currency; coinage; numismatics

e6f49abd-8e7a-5131-a593-cada7ee6ab5e.archival: *L'Esposizione di Parigi del 1878 illustrata*, Sonzogno Editore, 1878, p. 63
e6f49abd-8e7a-5131-a593-cada7ee6ab5e.keywords: Exposition universelle de Paris; industrialisation; pavillion; exhibition building; Moorish city; exhibitions and urban spaces; Moorish city; Islamic architecture; reinterpretation; exoticism; reproduction; model; suq; curiosities; French; Jews; magazine

e6f49abd-8e7a-5131-a593-cada7ee6ab5e.description2: International Exhibition in Paris, 1878. Tunisia is represented by the creation of different bazaars. The reporter's descriptions of Cattan's Bazaar report mainly religious objects such as wooden rosary beads, mother-pearl crosses and the biblical plant, the Rose of Jericho. The Ben Athia Bazaar displayed cultural objects from Tunisia: luxury arms, rich materials, embroidery, perfumes of roses, bronze and enamelled jewellery. The Eskenazi bazaar displayed various antique objects.

e714183d-faa1-5c38-bf56-e05a8f41f61e.keywords: Porte de France; Tunis medina; European quarter
e714183d-faa1-5c38-bf56-e05a8f41f61e.description2: This copy of a beautiful watercolour from Charles Lallemand's book *Tunis et ses Environs* shows the Porte de la Mer, or the Porte de France, around which both European settlers and Tunisian residents are gathered. Its location was strategic, as it led to both the Tunis medina and the European quarter.

e794e773-3653-5861-a65a-803eb3349875.description2: The trademark of the company “Smalto Tripoline” (a factory producing enamels and paintings), based in Verona (Veneto, the same region as Venice).

e89aa553-0859-53ef-ad91-bdaddb8ac231.name: *Hüdavendigar* Paper in Armenian
e89aa553-0859-53ef-ad91-bdaddb8ac231.description2: After the *Tanzimat* (reforms), newspapers in Arabic, Persian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Albanian, Kurdish, English, French, Italian and German began appearing in the Ottoman Empire. Some of them were bilingual as Turkish-Greek, Turkish-Armenian and Turkish-Arabic. *Hüdavendigar* was a provincial newspaper of Bursa and it was first published on 19 February 1869. The same year, starting with the 80th issue, the back page was printed in Armenian. The paper was published twice (Wednesday and Saturday) and then four times a week. It was 50 x 25 cm. Subscription for a year was 100 kuruş, for six months was 50 kuruş and one issue was 20 para (1/2 kuruş). It continued to be published until 1953 under different names.

e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.name: Arabic eye liner, *kohl* and perfume container
e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.author: Huda Kilani
e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.description2: Padded bag to hold three small brass bottles of Arab eye-liner, perfumes and essential oils. It was used as a wall decoration. Decorated with silk tassels, glass beads, Egyptian and Ottoman coins. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to settle in the Jordanian territory for these purposes. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of the area in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

e92c5fac-cccf-5730-b2e6-c7774c2761e7.name: The paved road between Beirut and Damascus
e92c5fac-cccf-5730-b2e6-c7774c2761e7.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Rita El Hachem
e92c5fac-cccf-5730-b2e6-c7774c2761e7.description2: This paved road was constructed between over a period of six years, between 1857 and 1863. It measured six metres in width and facilitated the circulation of horse-drawn carriages owned by the "diligence" transportation company.

e93e2356-ce89-5c16-b735-40f476c4b07d.name: Gustave Eiffel. The Eiffel Tower in 1889.
e93e2356-ce89-5c16-b735-40f476c4b07d.description2: Today, the Eiffel Tower is one of the great symbols of Paris and of France. This metal structure, a huge technological achievement in and of itself, was constructed by Gustave Eiffel (1823–1923) for the Exposition Universelle (world fair) of 1889, which celebrated the centenary of the French revolution. Many of his contemporaries, such as Guy de Maupassant, considered the structure hideous and called for its demolition. This drawing recalls the tower's function as a symbol of the vitality of French industry, highlighting its exceptional size and its proximity to the great Palais de l'Industrie, which housed the Dôme Central, the first building to use electricity on a large-scale.

e99ec60f-9439-5be8-b2c8-63118d0cc859.name: Photograph showing Beirut port after expansion
e99ec60f-9439-5be8-b2c8-63118d0cc859.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
e99ec60f-9439-5be8-b2c8-63118d0cc859.description2: This photograph shows the expanded docks and bunkers of Beirut port following the expansion works in 1890. This expansion made the port the largest of the Middle East.

ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.name: *Turkish ladies buying jewellery*
ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
ea56c676-8f35-5489-88dc-00a76f28ef9d.description2: This watercolour, completed in 1873, shows three elegantly dressed society ladies, their faces concealed by a light veil, visiting the shop of a jeweller, his wares displayed in a small multi-tiered glass case placed on the low platform in front. While one of the ladies is seated on a carpet at the entrance to the shop to examine a pearl necklace that the old, bespectacled proprietor has offered her, her two companions wait outside and shield her to some extent from curious eyes. Vittorio Amadeo, 5th Count Preziosi (1816-1882) was an artist of Maltese origin, who left for the Middle East in the early 1840s. He settled in Istanbul as a diplomatic translator and artist, specialising in touristic scenes, vistas and types

Appreciated more in France than in Italy, and initially excluded from Italian orders, it was reintroduced when the France decided to display it within other French works.

f0157113-5673-5605-86fe-951af8c08ff8.name: Map of Aden
f0157113-5673-5605-86fe-951af8c08ff8.author: Maria Francesca Carvelli (MWNF)
f0157113-5673-5605-86fe-951af8c08ff8.archival: *The Gulf of Aden Pilot ... Compiled from memoires of Officers of the Indian Navy, by ... C. Y. Ward*, *Sailing Directions. Aden*, London, Hydrographic Office, 1882, second edition, with additions
f0157113-5673-5605-86fe-951af8c08ff8.keywords: Trade; route; port; Great Britain; India; coffee; Red Sea; Yemen; Mocha; British settlement on the route to India; communication; telegraph; telegraph between ports; Suez Canal; Arab Peninsula
f0157113-5673-5605-86fe-951af8c08ff8.description2:
*The Gulf of Aden Pilot* included sailing indications and directions for navigation of the Suez Canal, the Gulf of Suez, the central route for steamships on the Red Sea, main ports on the Red Sea and directions for navigation through the Gulf of Aden, for a safe navigation.  
After the opening of the Suez Canal, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden were becoming increasingly important as maritime routes for communication and trade to the East. Reliable knowledge of routes, harbours, accomodation, supply stations, telegraph lines between the ports, winds, currents of the whole area was therefore of fundamental importance. The book also provides some information about communication and trade. For example, it states that Aden was declared a free port in 1850 and in the following years replaced Mokha as the main port for coffee trade.

f055e40d-1750-5d91-b228-ce1475837c25.name: Theresian thaler
f055e40d-1750-5d91-b228-ce1475837c25.keywords: coin; coinage; currency; numismatics; Arabian Peninsula; Najd; mint
f055e40d-1750-5d91-b228-ce1475837c25.description2: The Maria Theresian Thaler, a large silver coin originally created by Queen (Empress) Maria Theresia, minted in Austria until 1890. It was used in the Arabic Peninsula as a means of payment. This coin was countersigned at the Arabian mint of Ras Bab el Mandeb in 1890.

f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.name: Headdress
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.author: Huda Kilani
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.keywords: Ottoman; Russian coins; pendent; red and green silk
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.materials: Silver, fabric, glass beads, coins; casting, welding, weaving
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.description2: Three bands of silver chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head and attached to a surrounding fabric patterned in minute beadwork and sewn with various Ottoman and Russian coins. From this head-piece hangs a long piece of cotton sewn with coins of the Ottoman Empire with a rectangular pendant and multiple red and green silk tassels on the back. Headdresses like this one were worn by married women, as silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride. The Ottoman and Russian coins reflect the social and economic situation of Jordan between the end of the 19th century and the early 20th century, when it was part of the Ottoman empire and it was influenced by population movements, demographic changes and trade with distant countries.

f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.name: *The Great Khan of Damascus*
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.provenance: England; published in Etching depicting *'The Great Khan At Damascus'*, first published in John Carne, *'Syria, The Holy Land, Asia Minor, &c'*, 1836–1838
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.artist: Painted by William Henry Bartlett; engraved by William H, Kelsall
f1948597-53b1-578c-8bd5-dbd5ac4ee6c3.description2: Damascus had long been a major commercial hub in the Middle East, with trading caravans converging on its numerous souqs from all over the Islamic world. Commercial complexes had already flourished in the 18th century and were an integral part of Ottoman modernisation projects in the 19th century. This image gives a wonderful impression of the activities within a traditional Near Eastern khan or market complex in the 19th century. Under high vaulted domes, man and beast are engaged in various activities. Pack animals bring wares or are being unloaded, traders discuss their wares, rest or ponder their accounts. A fountain in the centre provides respite and coolness. On the second floor, figures are visible at the balconies, overlooking the activities below. The print was originally published in Volume I, p. 49, of 'Syria, The Holy Land, Asia Minor &c', printed in 3 series over 2 volumes, drawn by William Henry Bartlett and William Purser, engraved by W. Kelsall, with descriptive text by John Carne. Published by Fisher and Son, with series I and II bound together.

f2f8e110-2548-568d-9481-67689f396cdc.name: Al-Zubarah
f2f8e110-2548-568d-9481-67689f396cdc.dates: 5th millennium BC; 18th century settlement; abandoned probably at the beginning of the 20th century
f2f8e110-2548-568d-9481-67689f396cdc.history:
Earliest human occupation near the site of al-Zubarah may date back as early as the Late Neolithic period (5th millennium BC). The ceramic assemblage recovered from al-Zubarah site itself is pointing to a possible Abbasid (8th – 9th century AD) occupation, prior to a Late Islamic village existing during the final period of the reign of Safavids in the upper Gulf region (18th century).  
According to the current knowledge, the major development of the town took place after the arrival of the Utub-tribe in northern Qatar. Al-Zubarah flowered during the 2nd half of the 18th century AD and played an important political role until it was totally destroyed after a major attack of Omani led forces in 1811.  
In a second phase of occupation after this event the city was considerably smaller. It never obtained the same importance than the 18th century settlement and by the beginning of the 20th century, the village was probably left abandoned.
f2f8e110-2548-568d-9481-67689f396cdc.description2:
The ruins of Al Zubarah are a traditionally well-known tourist destination in Qatar.  
Recognized as an archaeological site as early as in the 1950es by a Danish led team of archaeologists, the first systematic archaeological excavations were conducted in 1983. Under the direction of the National Museum of Qatar, the Qatari team uncovered several structures in the northern part of the ruins. Later on, the attention was turned to what was identified as the suq area and the inner quarters.

f310be0c-2e4a-5a7a-ab0c-baaa41091e32.name: *Dokhla* (wedding dress)
f310be0c-2e4a-5a7a-ab0c-baaa41091e32.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
f310be0c-2e4a-5a7a-ab0c-baaa41091e32.keywords: Embroidery from Nabeul; sequins and gold thread
f310be0c-2e4a-5a7a-ab0c-baaa41091e32.materials: Embroidered fabric with gold-plated silver thread
f310be0c-2e4a-5a7a-ab0c-baaa41091e32.description2: This tunic is entirely embroidered with gold-plated silver thread. This is the most important element of the marriage ceremony (jelwa) in Nabeul (Tunisia). The rectangular tunic's splendour comes from its incredibly rich embroidery, which is made of various different silk ribbons, all embellished with tal. In fact, the embroidery entirely covers the fabric itself. The breast and belt areas are embroidered with sequins and gold thread. The tunic is calf-length, and a luxurious pair of silk trousers can be seen beneath, covered in gold embroidery to match the sleeves. In addition to this, one of the bride's many items of jewellery is a great chain of golden rings, a rihana, which she wears with a large necklace made of a scented material. Lastly, the bride's head is covered by an embroidered veil made of muslin and silk.

f398bf92-d6b1-56a3-bb47-793d5811643e.name: Models of traditional agricultural environment in Egypt and Sudan and the life in the Egyptian oases at Fu`ad Agricultural Museum
f398bf92-d6b1-56a3-bb47-793d5811643e.dates: 16 January 1938 (Photos taken during the inauguration of the museum)
f398bf92-d6b1-56a3-bb47-793d5811643e.description2: The Fu`ad Agriculture Museum was considered the first of its kind in the Middle East and the Arab World during the 1930s. It was inaugurated during the time of King Faruq, the son of King Fu`ad, and houses a large number of collections related to agricultural and rural environments, as well as agricultural plants and animals.

f62eb2d5-765a-5d02-9c15-324361c4a2e6.name: *The Mansion of Alexandros Lukas Benakis in Alexandria*
f62eb2d5-765a-5d02-9c15-324361c4a2e6.author: Maria Dimitriadou
f62eb2d5-765a-5d02-9c15-324361c4a2e6.description2: Black and white photos on a family album depicting the mansion of Alexander Lucas Benakis near Alexandria. Photographer unknown.

f659e676-c7e7-5974-ace5-795fdd1ed49b.name: *Bayt Lisbuna, Damascus*
f659e676-c7e7-5974-ace5-795fdd1ed49b.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
f659e676-c7e7-5974-ace5-795fdd1ed49b.author: Stefan Weber
f659e676-c7e7-5974-ace5-795fdd1ed49b.second_name: Inhabitants in the courtyard demonstrating the new style of decoration and clothing
f659e676-c7e7-5974-ace5-795fdd1ed49b.description2: The Bayt Lisbuna saw two major construction phases. The existing structures date from the 19th century (around 1810) and were remodelled after 1865 and 1872. This house of a Jewish family like many other houses of Muslim or Christian families underwent major changes in style and plan at the end of the 19th and beginning of the 20th centuries. Several thousand private homes were adopted to the new modern style, with a radical change in techniques and forms of decoration. While still being a Damascene courtyard house these monuments of private taste became witness of a comprehensive urban change in the light of an entangled modernity.

f8e91c25-98ab-5b7c-8cb2-16ce5beb2795.name: 25 Syrian Piastres
f8e91c25-98ab-5b7c-8cb2-16ce5beb2795.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
f8e91c25-98ab-5b7c-8cb2-16ce5beb2795.keywords: Commerce; trade; Currency; Coins; coinage; Numismatics
f8e91c25-98ab-5b7c-8cb2-16ce5beb2795.description2: This 25 piastres bank note was printed by Bradbury Wilkinson and Co (BWC) without a watermark.

f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.name: Cross chain
f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.author: Huda Kilani
f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.description2: A cross of silver on a silver chain known with the folkloric name “heal of gazelle”, worn by Christian women. Silver was the most common jewellery; only rich people used gold. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated religious composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also demonstrates personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.name: Yemeni dagger
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.author: Huda Kilani
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.keywords: double edged blade; hilts; geometric designs; silver filigree; suspension rings; arms; armours; metalwork; fashion; accessories
f986df26-3b71-5c3e-8d5b-1a8c60864ea5.description2: A dagger with a double-edged blade, an oblong-head hilt and silver filigree work in geometric designs; it is carried on a woollen belt with leather strap-work, usually with six asymmetrical suspension rings. Yemeni and Hijazi daggers have different shapes and their diffusion on the territory of Jordan shows how population movements, trade and exchange were common in the area.

fa8521f5-5b5a-5099-8913-7567fa1ba0ab.name: A moneylender's kit
fa8521f5-5b5a-5099-8913-7567fa1ba0ab.description2: In the first half of the 19th century, before the first banks were founded in Wallachia and Moldavia, moneylenders were the ones who dealt with money loaning and with currency exchange, in an economy which did not have yet a national coin. In Romanian they used to be called "zarafi", a term borrowed from the Turkish language. Most of them were Greek, Armenian and Jewish. They often travelled abroad to buy money, one of their main destinations being Istanbul.

faa81141-8f06-589d-906c-e5429a4e007b.name: Pipe
faa81141-8f06-589d-906c-e5429a4e007b.description: Meerschaum, sepiolite or écume de mer, is a porous mineral founded chiefly in Anatolia. Highly valued in pipe manufacturing since the late 18th century, the most famous meerschaum pipes in 19th century were those from Vienna or Paris. Due to commercial competition, new techniques were introduced. This pipe is an example of a patented French production that reproduced meerschaum pipes and cut the production price. This pipe in the shape of a young man’s head is not functional and merely decorative, and was collected by Antonio del Valle y Serrano, marquis of Villa-Huerta, in Mâcon (France), were he also collected souvenirs related to the famous poet Lamartine.
faa81141-8f06-589d-906c-e5429a4e007b.author: Cecilia Casas Desantes

fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.name: *Suqs*
fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.history:
The *suqs* of the Tunis medina, particularly those specialising by trade, play an important economic role in the city. Some examples are:  
  
• Suq el-Chaouchiya (selling chechias, woollen hats). Founded by the community of Muslims who had been expelled from Spain in the 17th century.  
• Suq Ettrouk (Turkish *suq*)  
• Suq el-Attarine (selling perfume).  
• Suq el-Nahas (selling brass and copper).  
• Suq el-Bey, founded by Hammouda Pacha (1781–1813)  
  
Located near the Zaytuna Mosque, these are the best *suqs* in the Tunis medina. The chechia industry particularly was at its peak here in the 19th century. Today, despite the undeniable decrease in demand, chechia production has survived by adapting to a new clientele, and has become the most popular artisanal Tunisian product with tourists.
fb62d82c-bb0f-5b66-b3bd-e65d7480fe70.description2: The *suqs* have preserved their beautiful architecture to this day, with different columns, pointed arches, and dark, cool rooms lit by the natural light streaming in through the holes in the whitewashed, vaulted ceilings. Located by the great Zaytuna Mosque, these *suqs* are always busy and full of life. Each *suq* is composed of a large central street, with a number of small shops and workshops opening up onto neighbouring narrower alleys, which are covered with vaulted ceilings, made with bricks arranged in different ways to form endless geometric patterns. The woodwork on the shops and their hobnailed doors, painted in a thousand colours and decorated with calligraphic designs, add to the *suq*'s spectacular appearance.

ffecc84b-856d-5f87-97de-682a1d90e53d.name: *View of Istanbul: the Valide Sultan Mosque and the port*
ffecc84b-856d-5f87-97de-682a1d90e53d.second_name: Taken from the collection *Photographies Positives* by Pascal Sébah
ffecc84b-856d-5f87-97de-682a1d90e53d.description2: Pascal Sébah (1823–1886) was a French photographer working in the Ottoman capital Constantinople, where he developed a successful trade selling photographs to European tourists and lovers of Orientalism. The great changes Constantinople underwent towards the end of the 19th century are evident in this image. The Valide Sutlan Mosque dominates the Eminönü port, which had become very prosperous during the Ottoman era thanks to active trading with the West. The construction of the Galata bridge, the Orient Express railway line, and the arrival of steam-boats also contributed to its development.
